ai-6f3953006a.headline: Anthropic sets IPO price range of $70 to $78 per share to reach an implied valuation of $1.404 trillion
ai-6f3953006a.fulltext:
Anthropic intends to push ahead with its IPO despite shakier markets and the broader pullback from AI investing.
The Claude-maker said in an updated IPO filing on Tuesday that it would be offering a total of 825 million Class A shares at an estimated price range of $70 to $78 per share. The sale is expected to raise anywhere from $57.75 billion to $64.35 billion.
The company could end up being worth a hefty $1.404 trillion if its shares list at the top of the price range, on a fully diluted basis. That would represent a significant jump up from the $965 billion valuation Anthropic reached in a May fundraise, but it’s still lower than the $2 trillion the company was reportedly targeting a couple months ago.
Separately, Anthropic said it had struck a deal to privately sell $26 billion of non-voting Class N stock at the IPO price to AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC. Google and Nvidia are investing $10 billion apiece.
All up, Anthropic estimates net proceeds to reach somewhere between $84.6 billion and $93.7 billion (the latter if the IPO underwriters exercise their option to buy additional shares).
Underwriters, including Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, will have the option to buy up to 123.75 million more shares from Anthropic at the IPO price.
As a public benefit corporation, the founders hold a Class F share with 50.1% of the voting power. The Long-Term Benefit Trust will also elect a board majority, so Class A buyers will have limited influence.
Anthropic intends to start trading on the Nasdaq close to November 19, per reporting from CNBC, under the ticker symbol “ANT.” The company expects up to 20% of the offering to be allocated to retail investors.
Anthropic also gave out a few new details in the updated filing. The company said its run-rate revenue reached $81 billion by the end of October, about $10 billion more than at the end of September.
Also, the filing now lists how many shares the company’s co-founders expect to sell in the IPO: CEO Dario Amodei, president and chairperson Daniela Amodei, chief compute officer Tom Brown, Anthropic Institute head Jack Clark, chief science officer Jared Kaplan, chief architect Sam McCandlish, and interpretability research lead Christopher Olah are all selling nearly 3.4 million shares each. At the $74 midpoint of the IPO price range, that would land them about $250 million each.
The updated filing also has a small but important change that hints at the company’s stance toward the Trump administration: The company at many points uses “super intelligence” and “SI” interchangeably with “artificial intelligence” and “AI,” citing Trump’s executive order from September that directed government departments and agencies to use that new terminology to refer to AI.
The company’s third-quarter revenue came in at $17 billion, and nine-month revenue was $33.2 billion. The company reported a nine-month net loss of $104 billion, with compute and infrastructure commitments hitting $900.9 billion. It has nearly $132 billion in cash and short-term investments.
OpenAI, Anthropic’s biggest rival, was reportedly valued at $1.25 trillion last week after it raised $11 billion, nearly half the $20 billion it had first tried to raise.
Note: This story has been updated with additional details and color from the updated IPO filing.

Australia to launch AI safety regulator after OpenAI's breach of a government portal
The regulator would enforce world-leading legislated AI standards that would apply to all frontier AI companies that want to operate in Australia, Albanese said.
Australia plans to create an artificial intelligence safety regulator in response to a breach of an Australian health department website by a rogue OpenAI agent in June, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Tuesday.
The regulator would enforce world-leading legislated AI standards that would apply to all frontier AI companies that want to operate in Australia, Albanese said. Financial penalties would apply, although the government has yet to detail those penalties.
-----------------------------------------------------------
The standards would include companies maintaining security controls across all stages of models' development and deployment, as well as identifying and managing serious risks. The standards also would mandate rapid notification to the government of incidents such as "misaligned behavior" conflicting with developers' intentions.
Australian government documents define frontier AI as the most sophisticated models at the cutting edge of current technological capability.
Albanese told OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman that the U.S. company took too long to inform the government in September that a rogue agent had infiltrated government websites three months earlier, which was the first occurrence of such a breach with the technology.
Information taken without authorization from the public-facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal on June 18 has since been made public. It is not clear whether the portal breach broke any Australian laws.
OpenAI apologized in September for the breach and its slow response.
"We are sorry and working to do better in the future," OpenAI said in a statement. "We also should have handled our response better."
Inquiry recommends possible criminal law changes
----------------------------------------------------
A government inquiry into the June breach made several recommendations including that the government consider changing the law.
Albanese said his government had accepted all the inquiry's recommendations, including for potential criminal law reform.
"The point is law needs to get ahead of and in some cases make sure that it catches up with what is a very fast-changing world. And to be clear, Australia is a first-mover in these areas," Albanese said.
The proposed AI regulator would follow Australia appointing an eSafety Commissioner in 2015. The office describes itself as the world's first government agency dedicated to keeping people safer online.
Since December last year, the commissioner has been enforcing a world-first ban on Australian children younger than 16 holding accounts on popular social media platforms.

ai-0336087d2a.headline: Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2.5 scores 96 percent sorting metal parts in a Mercedes-Benz assembly pilot
ai-0336087d2a.fulltext:
Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2.5 scores 96 percent sorting metal parts in a Mercedes-Benz assembly pilot
Key Points
- Google Deepmind introduced Gemini Robotics 2.5, a new VLA model it says performs 30 to 100 percent better than its own previous baselines depending on the task type.
- On active Mercedes-Benz production lines in Hungary and Germany, Apptronik's humanoid robot Apollo 2 sorted metal parts with a reported success rate of 96 percent.
- Google Deepmind uses its language model Gemini 4 Argon as a simulation engine for training and released the open-source benchmark ASIMOV-Jailbreak to test the safety of robotics models.
Google Deepmind has unveiled a new AI model for robot control. In a pilot test on active Mercedes-Benz production lines, a humanoid robot reportedly achieved a 96 percent success rate.
Google Deepmind has introduced Gemini Robotics 2.5, a vision-language-action model (VLA) that processes visual information, understands language instructions, and translates them into robot movements. The model builds on its predecessor, introduced earlier this year, which was designed to give robots full-body control for the first time.
Google Deepmind says it tested the model on more than 200 tasks, including serving food with tongs and pipetting liquids. Compared to the company's own previous baselines, it reportedly achieves a 30 to 100 percent higher success rate depending on the task type and completes tasks 20 to 30 percent faster.
The model is designed to work with different robot types, including Apptronik's humanoid robot Apollo 2 with a five-fingered hand that has 22 degrees of freedom, and the Franka Duo platform with two-finger parallel grippers.
Google Deepmind tests the model on active Mercedes-Benz production lines
Together with Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz, Google Deepmind tested the model on active production lines in Kecskemét, Hungary, and Sindelfingen, Germany. The Apollo 2 robot handled kitting: it sorted metal parts from bulk bins and placed them into trays in the order needed for each vehicle on the assembly line. Two AI models worked in tandem. Gemini Robotics ER monitored the workflow, while Gemini Robotics 2.5 controlled hands and arms.
Video: Google
Google Deepmind reports a 96 percent success rate for this pilot test. Apptronik CEO Jeff Cardenas said the models improved significantly within a few weeks of post-training and successfully transitioned to Mercedes production with minimal performance loss.
New Safety Benchmark Against Jailbreaks
According to Google Deepmind, Gemini Robotics 2.5 uses real-time control that enables the robot to avoid physical hazards while performing a task. In its own evaluations, safe task completion improved by 33 percent near obstacles and by 43 percent near people.
In addition, Google Deepmind has published the open-source ASIMOV-Jailbreak benchmark on Hugging Face. It contains hundreds of prompts that disguise unsafe requests in dozens of scenes and is designed to test whether robotics models can be tricked into performing dangerous actions. According to the company, Google’s own model, Gemini 4 Argon, achieves a jailbreak resistance of 99.5 percent, compared to 82 percent for its predecessor, Gemini Robotics ER 2.
Argon Language Model Generates Training Data via Simulation
During the development of Gemini Robotics 2.5, Google Deepmind used its own language model, Gemini 4 Argon, as a simulation engine. Argon can generate thousands of simulated training runs from a real camera scene and create a digital twin. In combination with real-world training demonstrations, this is intended to help the robot generalize more quickly to new scenes and objects. Argon can also derive hypotheses about the causes of errors from video recordings and test improvements in simulation and on the actual robot.
According to Google Deepmind, Gemini Robotics 2.5 is being rolled out to partners Agile, Apptronik, and Mercedes-Benz.

climate-energy-1fafae0b34.headline: China curbs expose India's solar, battery machinery dependence; manufacturers scout for alternatives
climate-energy-1fafae0b34.fulltext:
India's dependence on China for machinery and technology used in upstream solar manufacturing — from ingots and wafers to cells — and battery-cell production is emerging as a major vulnerability for its clean energy manufacturing ambitions.
With access to Chinese supplies becoming increasingly uncertain amid frequent export curbs, Indian manufacturers are exploring equipment and technology partnerships with suppliers in other countries to diversify their sourcing, Moneycontrol has learnt.
Industry representatives said Indian solar manufacturers had faced intermittent restrictions this year on access to Chinese manufacturing technology, equipment and technical support, affecting plans to set up upstream manufacturing facilities for wafers, ingots and polysilicon.
More recently, on October 16, China introduced an interim pre-export registration requirement for specified solar technology transfers while proposing to prohibit or restrict exports of 12 photovoltaic manufacturing technologies. The proposed controls, covering selected polysilicon, wafer and cell manufacturing technologies and associated equipment, are expected to be taken up for a decision by the Chinese government after November 15.
India has already built substantial solar module manufacturing capacity, with supply in this segment outpacing domestic demand. Cell manufacturing capacity is also expanding rapidly, with Union Minister for New and Renewable Energy Pralhad Joshi saying it is expected to reach 70 GW by December 2026 and cross 100 GW by May-June 2027.
But, the next focus for the industry is deeper integration of the supply chain through domestic manufacturing of polysilicon, ingots and wafers — the key inputs used to produce solar cells. This is where India's manufacturing capabilities remain particularly limited, leaving expansion plans vulnerable to restrictions on access to Chinese technology and equipment.
To mitigate the risk of supply disruptions, the industry is scouting for technology and equipment partnerships beyond China. Subrahmanyam Pulipaka, Chief Executive Officer of the National Solar Energy Federation of India (NSEFI), told Moneycontrol that manufacturers were exploring tie-ups with suppliers in Germany, South Korea, Japan, Italy and Australia. However, the alternatives remain limited, as some manufacturers in these countries also outsource production to China, he said.
Amit Manohar, Secretary General of the Indian Solar Manufacturers Association (ISMA), said Indian manufacturers were working to build resilience through diversified technology sourcing, global partnerships and stronger in-house engineering capabilities.
“Companies are increasingly exploring equipment and technology partnerships across Europe, Japan, Taiwan and other markets, reducing concentration risks. This diversified approach ensures greater supply chain flexibility, technological adaptability and long-term manufacturing competitiveness,” Manohar told Moneycontrol.
Building domestic machinery-making capabilities, however, will take time. “It will take at least three years in the best-case scenario and up to five years realistically,” Pulipaka said.
The dependence also leaves Indian manufacturers exposed to pricing pressure across the solar value chain. Pulipaka said China had raised cell prices while lowering module prices when Indian manufacturers expanded module production, squeezing their margins.
“Now, as India catches up in cell manufacturing, China has adopted a similar approach by raising wafer prices while lowering cell prices. This makes it costlier for Indian manufacturers to produce cells while allowing cheaper Chinese cells to compete with domestic products, putting local manufacturers at a disadvantage," he said, while adding that the strategy was aimed at choking India's domestic solar manufacturing industry.
A NITI Aayog report prepared with Crisil Intelligence found that capital goods used in polysilicon, wafer and cell manufacturing are concentrated largely in China. Separately, a January report by The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI) found that more than 90% of high-end solar manufacturing equipment, including furnaces, PECVD/ALD tools and diamond-wire saws, is imported.
The exposure extends to batteries as well. India imported $1.5 billion worth of battery-cell manufacturing machinery from China in 2022, according to an analysis by the International Institute for Sustainable Development (IISD). China was the leading supplier across several equipment categories, including calendaring, slitting, electrolyte-filling and cell-formation machinery.

work-careers-abd5935338.headline: Qantas AI Jobs are Coming to India as Outsourcing Deal Affects 850 Roles
work-careers-abd5935338.fulltext:
Australian airline Qantas expects around 850 corporate roles to be affected over the coming years under a new outsourcing partnership with Accenture, with much of the work moving to the consultancy's teams in India.
Some services currently handled by Qantas employees will move to Accenture, with delivery split between teams in India and Australia. The first changes are expected by mid-2027.
Qantas said the partnership would modernise the technology and data systems supporting its operations. Its existing infrastructure includes more than 1,000 legacy applications built up over decades that were not designed to work together.
"That means fundamentally redesigning how the work behind our airline gets done, so it is simpler, more connected, and keeps getting better, with automation and AI built in from the start," Qantas Group CEO Vanessa Hudson said in a statement. Accenture will invest upfront to accelerate the modernisation of Qantas's data platforms.
Qantas said it would seek to redeploy affected employees where possible, including through reskilling and retraining, and provide ongoing support.
Qantas is not the first Australian company to restructure its workforce as a result of an Accenture partnership. In February 2026, telecommunications company Telstra said 209 roles were expected to go from its $700 million data and AI joint venture with Accenture, with some work moving to the venture's team in India. The telco was also considering a separate 440 job cuts linked to outsourcing work to Infosys.
Telstra's partnership with Accenture was also aimed at modernising its data infrastructure and advancing its AI strategy, with the joint venture taking on a role in the company's technology transformation.

india-e05690e630.headline: China Wants India’s Market. Does It Want India’s Industrial Rise? - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
india-e05690e630.source: The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
india-e05690e630.fulltext:
China’s latest export controls could complicate its economic rapprochement with India. On October 19, Beijing announced export controls on strategic heavy construction and engineering machinery – including tunnel-boring machines and walking excavators – with tougher licensing requirements for destinations involved in disputes with China.
For India, whose metro and high-speed rail projects rely on such machinery, the implications are immediate, including a delay in deliveries for machines manufactured in China by a German company. The new rules, effective November 18, give Beijing another lever over India’s industrial ambitions.
Three days earlier, China proposed adding 40 technologies, including advanced solar manufacturing processes, to its prohibited or restricted export lists. These moves follow years of tightening controls on critical minerals and industrial technology. Several consequential measures, notably the 2025 rare earth restrictions, emerged amid China’s confrontation with the United States.
Yet India has felt their effects acutely. Magnet shortages disrupted Indian automakers, while electronics and clean tech manufacturers struggled to secure equipment and expertise. China’s regulatory arsenal, though developed largely for great power competition, has acquired growing significance for India’s industrial future.
China’s export controls could stymie Indian progress into higher-value manufacturing. India’s production-linked incentives (PLIs) are encouraging investment in batteries, solar energy, and advanced manufacturing. Yet moving into more sophisticated production requires specialized machinery, engineering expertise, and technical know-how, much of which still comes from China. Restrictions on those transfers threaten to slow India’s efforts to develop domestic capabilities.
Chinese strategic commentators have long questioned the wisdom of supplying technology and machinery that could help India emerge as an industrial competitor. Beijing has also challenged Indian subsidies for batteries, EVs, and solar manufacturing at the World Trade Organization. China’s growing list of restrictions on technology exports gives Beijing more ways to act on those longstanding concerns.
Yet restricting India carries a price. India is a major and growing market for Chinese manufacturers, many of which face brutal competition at home and trade barriers in the United States and Europe. Bilateral trade reached a record $155.6 billion in 2025, overwhelmingly in China’s favor: China exported $135.9 billion worth of goods to India. Chinese machinery, components, and expertise are integral to India’s industrial expansion. Therefore, the companies selling them have powerful reasons to keep doing business.
That tension is evident in Chinese-language commentary. Some writers warn that sweeping restrictions would send Indian customers to German, Japanese, or Korean suppliers and accelerate India’s efforts to develop domestic alternatives. Others advocate a more selective approach: continue supplying commercially valuable equipment while guarding the technologies and manufacturing know-how that sustain China’s industrial lead. Yet industrial equipment is a long-term commitment. If Indian buyers cannot count on spare parts, upgrades, and technical support, cheaper Chinese machinery becomes a riskier investment.
The timing is particularly uncomfortable for New Delhi. After years of restrictions on Chinese investment since the Galwan clash in 2020, India eased approval procedures in March for selected manufacturing sectors, including capital goods, electronic components, and solar inputs. Its stated aim was to attract investment, gain access to technology, and connect Indian firms with global supply chains. New Delhi is easing access to Chinese investment just as Beijing tightens controls over technology transfers. Even a Chinese-funded factory approved by India may struggle to obtain the production technology it needs from China.
India may continue expanding its manufacturing base using Chinese equipment. But acquiring the engineering capabilities to produce more sophisticated technologies at home will be increasingly difficult if Beijing restricts access to the expertise it needs.
Beijing, of course, has a calculation of its own. Tighter controls could slow India’s emergence as an industrial competitor while preserving its reliance on Chinese suppliers. Yet excessive restrictions may eventually drive Indian manufacturers toward alternative partners, even at greater cost. Beijing could find that protecting its industrial advantage today comes at the expense of its commercial opportunities in India tomorrow.

other-interests-6209ded959.headline: Oil prices are so high that CO2 emissions from fossil fuels are dropping
other-interests-6209ded959.fulltext:
The U.S. war with Iran has raised fossil fuel prices so much that the resulting drop in oil demand has put the world on track to see a rare dip in carbon emissions from these sources in 2026.
Between 2019 and 2025, carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels grew by about 0.8 percent annually, according to a new study published in Nature Climate Change. But 2026 is set to buck that trend: high oil prices, as well as the continued rise of green technology—solar power, wind and electric cars—will cause a “short-term” 0.4 percent drop, according to the study.
“The high petrol prices following the war in Iran are reducing oil use and keeping emissions low,” says the study’s lead author Corinne Le Quéré, a professor of climate change science at the University of East Anglia in England. “But that’s not the whole story: The expansion of renewable energy has progressed a lot in recent years, led by China. And [along with electric vehicles], this is offsetting two thirds of the growing demand for energy.”

The findings come as the United Nations’ climate talks get underway in Antalya, Türkiye, and during a year marred by global temperature extremes and climate disasters. This year is on track to be among the hottest on record.
The drop in emissions is also notable because it is the first annual reduction since the COVID pandemic, when emissions dropped by an estimated 5 percent or so, Le Quéré says. Researchers also measured a small decrease in emissions after the 2008 recession. “However, in both cases, emissions rebounded the year after,” Le Quéré says.
If oil prices return to their prewar levels, Le Quéré and her colleagues expect to see emissions rise once more. But the “rebound” could be countered by further adding renewable energy to the world’s portfolio, she adds.
“We show that to tackle climate change and guarantee that global fossil emissions decrease durably, the expansion of renewable energy and electric vehicles need to accelerate further,” Le Quéré says.

ai-d08cd32469.headline: NVIDIA Scandal & AI Selloff In the US: India’s Neocloud Boom Faces Twin Tests
ai-d08cd32469.fulltext: The alleged espionage scandal involving NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and the growing scrutiny of the chipmaker’s business dealings with China have added another layer of uncertainty to the global AI infrastructure market already facing questions about its financing model. At the same time, political and regulatory resistance to data centre expansion in the US could slow infrastructure investment, putting pressure on companies that have borrowed heavily to build capacity. While unrelated, these developments present two separate risks to the investment model underpinning the AI infrastructure boom. The first is already visible in the American stock market. Investors have been selling shares of US neocloud companies since September, with CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN witnessing sharp corrections. The selling intensified through October and into November, as concerns mounted over the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending and the debt these companies have taken on. The selloff has only intensified talk of an AI bubble, and neoclouds in India face the risk of getting caught in the middle. Neoclouds – AI infrastructure providers that offer GPU-as-a-service - have emerged as an important part of NVIDIA's AI ecosystem. They provide GPU compute to customers that may not have the scale or resources to build their own infrastructure. Neocloud business models are capital-intensive, with GPU procurement, data centre capacity, and financing arrangements determining how quickly they can scale up. NVIDIA has played a significant role in supporting this ecosystem through strategic investments and financing arrangements, helping expand the market for its chips beyond traditional hyperscalers. India is increasingly becoming part of this infrastructure buildout. That buildout serves two demand pools. One is subsidised compute for domestic startups, researchers and institutions under the IndiaAI Mission, which had onboarded over 45,000 GPUs by June 2026. By August, it had approved 237 projects for subsidised compute, with 93.18 lakh GPU hours sanctioned. The other is commercial workloads from customers willing to pay for guaranteed capacity. The first highlights the scale of the government programme, but sanctioned hours do not necessarily translate into sustained usage. To justify their spending, India’s neoclouds are betting on the second. Among the main Indian players, Yotta plans to spend over $7 Bn on AI infrastructure by the end of FY27 and is targeting a $1.5 Bn IPO, partly to repay debt. ESDS went to the market after the cost of the GPU servers it planned to buy rose from ₹25 Lakh to ₹1.8 Cr. E2E Networks, meanwhile, reported a 411% year-on-year jump in Q2 revenue. Besides these, the likes of NxtGen, NeevCloud and Neysa are also building their neocloud infrastructure in India in anticipation of a big adoption wave. US giant CoreWeave is also entering India as the sole tenant of a planned 240 MW AdaniConneX data centre campus. However, any sustained pressure on its financing or expansion plans could have implications for the project. If concerns in the US around data centre build-up trickle down to India, neoclouds will be one of the first to get hit as a lot of their build-up depends on institutional funding commitment. The question is whether Indian companies will continue to enjoy the financial backing and attract customer commitments to withstand the headwinds if and when they come. No Anchor Customers In India The investment case for US AI infrastructure companies is underpinned by large customers such as Meta and OpenAI, whose scale and long-term compute requirements offer some visibility into future demand. These anchor customers make it easier for infrastructure providers to secure financing and justify large upfront investments. Indian neoclouds, however, do not yet have comparable customer base to underwrite their expansion plans. International customers now account for 75-80% of Yotta’s customer base, partly because they are willing to pay more. Within India, however, the IndiaAI Mission is emerging as an important source of demand, although it utilised less than half its FY26 outlay of ₹10,000 Cr, which has directly impacted hardware procurement and deployment timelines, as Neysa mentioned in one of its blogs. A recent Moneycontrol report highlighted a mismatch in the Indian market: some GPUs are underused, while startups and researchers say fragmented capacity, allocation delays and the type of hardware on offer can make suitable compute difficult to obtain. A headline GPU count may therefore obscure both the quality of available clusters and the path from allocation to actual use. The mismatch makes domestic demand hard to read. The demand exists, but it does not always reach the neoclouds that have built capacity for it. Even well-funded companies are waiting. Juspay, which buys GPUs with its own cash, has been “given commitments that it will take three to six months” to receive them, co-founder and COO Sheetal Lalwani said at a media briefing. When large customers buy and run their own hardware, and smaller ones struggle to find suitable clusters, aggregate capacity figures say little about how much will turn into long-term, paying contracts for neoclouds. Can government-backed compute requirements offer the kind of long-term revenue visibility that hyperscaler contracts provide in the US? Or will Indian neoclouds remain dependent on international customers to sustain utilisation and justify their infrastructure investments? GPU infrastructure requires substantial upfront capital, while the returns depend on sustained utilisation, predictable demand and long-term customer commitments. Notably, government-led regulations as well as citizen pushback could limit data centre build; it even emerged as a major factor for voters in the recent US midterm elections. For Indian neocloud players, which are increasingly catering to foreign and especially US-based clients, could suffer a trickle-down effect. Neocloud stocks, those of Coreweave, Nebius and Iren, among others, battered after the Democratic win in the recent elections. Closer home, ESDS and E2E stocks are already suffering from the second order impact of the sharp selloff in US tech stocks, following the mid-term results. On November 9, ESDS closed at approximately ₹1,147.25, against a September 24 high of ₹1,864.35, while E2E Networks ended at around ₹490.50, significantly lower than its October 14 high of ₹769. The NVIDIA Question NVIDIA’s role in the neocloud ecosystem goes beyond supplying GPUs. Its investments, financing arrangements and partnerships with infrastructure providers have helped bring new compute capacity online. But the relationship varies across Indian companies. NeevCloud said its engagement with NVIDIA covers technical planning, GPU availability and deployment readiness. Procurement, financing and customer contracts are separate arrangements. The company acknowledged the concentration risk of relying on a single technology provider, but said it ties investments to customer commitments and available financing. “The market correction reinforces the need for discipline. We assess each project on its commercial viability and phase investments accordingly,” Narendra Sen, founder of NeevCloud and RackBank Datacenters, told Inc42. ESDS said it has no direct commercial or financing relationship with NVIDIA. The company buys systems from OEMs and system integrators such as Supermicro, Dell, Lenovo and WWT. It has also signed a $1.25 Bn, seven-year agreement with Australia’s Sharon AI. Sharon AI owns and operates an 8,000-GPU cluster, which ESDS uses to serve its domestic and global customers. ESDS plans to explore similar partnerships. “I would separate technology dependence from financial dependence,” said Piyush Somani, founder of ESDS. He pointed out that all of ESDS’s deployed GPU capacity runs on NVIDIA. Financing is a different matter. ESDS commits capex only after a customer has paid at least 35% of the project cost, and only then does it place orders with OEMs or system integrators, Somani said. Both companies say financing for neocloud centres is getting more selective. Lenders and investors now favour projects with confirmed customers, predictable revenues and substantial upfront advances. Sen added that older GPUs could face more pricing pressure as newer generations arrive. This is where the economic model gets complicated. NVIDIA has offered neoclouds worldwide a revenue-sharing and credit-support model in July, but later paused some of the deals, as reported by The Wall Street Journal. Yotta is exploring similar structures where partners fund and own the GPUs, while the company installs and operates them in its data centres and signs customer contracts. In April, the two companies deepened their partnership, adding another $2.8 Bn to an agreement that was initially valued at $500 Mn. Such partnership models depend on GPU rental prices holding up. If compute prices fall or older GPUs lose value faster than expected, who absorbs the loss: the neocloud, the customer or the financing partner? The Jensen Huang Overhang NVIDIA’s chips, software stack and partnerships shape how quickly new compute capacity comes online. That is one of the reasons The Economist has called it the “central bank of AI”. This also highlights growing concerns about the AI ecosystem’s dependence on NVIDIA. On November 8, NVIDIA’s board launched an independent investigation into reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Huang has acknowledged an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be spying for the Chinese government. The NVIDIA board, however, has maintained that it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. Questions about her alleged links to Chinese intelligence, and what they mean for NVIDIA’s China business, remain open. For Indian neoclouds, the direct exposure is less about a change in NVIDIA’s leadership and more about their dependence on globally-sourced GPUs and NVIDIA’s software ecosystem. The Government of India has said its compute ecosystem currently relies on globally-sourced GPUs and any change in chip availability, export controls, pricing or allocation could affect deployment schedules and project economics. There is no evidence yet that the controversy has affected NVIDIA’s relationships with Indian neoclouds. But any fallout for its leadership, China business or financing strategy would hit an ecosystem that leans heavily on NVIDIA’s technology. There are concerns regarding what a potential wider restructuring of NVIDIA might mean for the neocloud business, especially if the build-up of data centres slows down in the US. Incidentally, NVIDIA is set to announce its third quarter earnings on November 17, 2026, and this will reveal much more about the underlying numbers for the data centre business. Will the corporate governance issues have an overhang on the stock till then? In February this year, the fear was that AI would trigger a SaaSpocalypse. Since then, models have advanced and the opportunities have grown bigger, but the concern now is whether the companies building AI infrastructure can carry the debt and capital commitments needed to keep this boom going.

ai-2800935556.headline: PSI is trying to make a business out of AI-driven scientific discovery
ai-2800935556.fulltext:
David Turturean, a recent MIT graduate and a member of the technical staff at the startup lab Physical Superintelligence (PSI), used early access to Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model to solve an 18-year-old problem about quantum computing.
“I’m totally accepting the idea that this might be the last paper I ever put out,” Turturean, who deferred plans to pursue a master’s at MIT’s prestigious computer science and AI lab to join PSI, told TechCrunch. “In a few months, like, why would you even put out a paper?”
The problem in question, the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, concerns the ability of quantum computers to solve problems faster than classical ones. Scott Aaronson, one of the two researchers who posed the problem, writes that he doesn’t quite understand the proof but that he believes it’s correct because it was autoformalized in Lean, a coding language for math, and explained by a team of top researchers with whom PSI shared the solution.
The solution appears to close the door on one avenue quantum computers could follow to solve certain difficult problems at high speed, but not all of them. “It’s a negative result that allows people to know, okay, we’re no longer looking there,” Turturean said.
More broadly, it reflects the upheaval in the scientific world caused by AI problem-solving.
“A proof of full [Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture] was one of the last remaining open problems in quantum query complexity that everyone seemed to agree was centrally important,” Aaronson, who described himself feeling satisfied, awestruck, disappointed, and fatigued by the news, wrote. “I was surprised, honestly, to see it missing from OpenAI’s Mathocalypse dump a few weeks ago. Surely they tried it, so was it really so much harder than all the problems that were solved?”
That’s a point in favor of PSI’s model, which is to solve scientific problems with specialized model harnesses and scaffolding.
“An effective kind of research system should have lots of things related to harnesses, lots related to tools, memory systems, simulation infrastructure,” PSI CEO Matt Pines told TechCrunch. “You want to be able to really go after a problem at breadth and depth, and be able to consider a wide range of potential alternatives.”
For now, the company’s revenue comes from using its tools to optimize data centers, simulating the variables of heat, power, water, sound — “where the performance of that site as well as its impact on the community are a direct function of its physics.” The long play, however, is converting theoretical physics breakthroughs into actual technologies.
“Six to nine months ago, when I was talking to investors, like I had to sort of stretch to validate that conditional, right? Like, ‘no, no, no, trust me, pretty soon, theoretical physics is going to be mostly the domain of machines,’” Pines said. “And it’s not there yet, but it’s on its way.”
Still, while AI has claimed important solutions in fields like mathematics and computer science where it’s possible to express them in validated code, doing so in less abstracted disciplines like the life sciences or physics has proven more difficult. Last week, the startup Discovered Materials released a $1 million grand challenge for researchers using AI to understand problems like superconductivity and heat dissipation.
“At the end of the day, physics is different than math because it’s the real world … nature gets a vote in your models of reality,” Pines said. He said the startup is focused on understanding how to take computational results and validate them with experiments in the most efficient way possible.
“If it’s a true fact of nature, that’s a trick that you can exploit,” Pines said. “You could build a device out of it, right? The AI suggests an idea; it allows you to do something in the world you weren’t able to do before … and so each of those are kind of loops that PSI is building.”
As “neolabs for science” become a pathway for potentially groundbreaking science, the participants are still figuring out what the standards are for this new world. Because PSI had to hold its result until Anthropic’s model was nearly ready for release, they were able to share it with relevant researchers to better understand it.
“As an academic, we wanted to play our role in doing things the right way,” Jim Halverson, a professor at Northeastern University who advises PSI, said. He’ll be attending a summit at MIT next week where leading physicists will try to hash out a response to the new pace of science. “Best practices are still emerging … We figured that transparency is a good way to go, and contacting experts is a good way to go.”
“We had some time to sit on it … and it was the first time that I actually took one of my AI-elicited solutions on print, and I read through it, and I was like, okay, how can I make this … be presented more naturally for a human?” Turturean, who said the academic community will expect him to be able to explain the result, told TechCrunch. “And I think it also made me realize, oh my God, the weight of what AI can do.”

ai-5b07820462.headline: Nvidia's model GR00T 2 watches humans on video, then imagines itself as the robot
ai-5b07820462.fulltext:
Nvidia's model GR00T 2 watches humans on video, then imagines itself as the robot
To teach robots new tasks, humans usually have to laboriously teleoperate them during training. Nvidia's new AI model GR00T 2 is designed to cut that effort by transferring human movements from videos to robotic arms.
To train a robot for new tasks, engineers usually spend hours remotely controlling the machines. This so-called teleoperation is expensive, slow, and needs its own data for every robot model. In a new research report on GR00T 2, Nvidia introduces a new AI foundation model designed to shorten this process.
Unlike previous approaches, including its predecessor GR00T 1, GR00T 2 doesn't translate camera images and language commands directly into motor movements. Nvidia says the software works as what the company calls a world-action model. It simultaneously calculates the next movement and a short video of the immediate future. The system predicts how the camera image should change when a robotic arm picks up an object, for example.
This video prediction should let the model transfer movement sequences between different robot form factors. Nvidia trained the system on a cluster with more than a thousand GB300 chips, including about 400,000 hours of video footage showing people performing various tasks while wearing head-mounted cameras.
To then teach a robot a new task, the researchers say it should be enough for a person to demonstrate the steps using data gloves, specialized hand grippers, or a finger exoskeleton. When these recordings are combined during training with general motion data from the target robot, the AI generates the robotic arm instead of the human arm in its video prediction and derives the matching control commands from that.
In lab tests, a robot with five-fingered hands was able to light a match, slice a banana, or toss packages onto a conveyor belt this way, without having been teleoperated for those specific tasks.
Success rates varied between 10 and 80 percent depending on the task. From a single video of a human hand movement, the system also learned to hammer nails by way of a computer simulation. For 50 selected tasks where the model already performed well after just a few examples, less than three minutes of conventional training was enough to raise the success rate from 40 to 95 percent.
A higher-level language model helps with errors but slows the robot down
For longer assembly work, Nvidia pairs the system with a higher-level AI language model like OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra. While GR00T 2 handles the gripping movements, the language model breaks the task into individual steps, color-codes grip points in the camera image, and launches helper routines when a part falls off.
When the researchers placed loose parts for toy models on a table in no particular order, the combined system assembled them in at least 97 percent of trials. Without the corrective language model and additional fine-tuning, the toy car assembly succeeded in only 23 out of 100 attempts. The team also trained precision tasks like plugging in network cables or chargers through repeated trial and error on the real device.
For bipedal robots, Nvidia developed the slimmed-down variant GR00T 2 Turbo, which processes fewer image details. It runs directly on the Jetson Thor onboard computer of a humanoid robot. In testing, the machine was able to scoop popcorn, clear tables, and wipe up liquids with a towel under its foot. That last task, though, succeeded in just under half of all attempts.
The research team identifies significant hurdles before the system is ready for reliable real-world use. The model doesn't yet process direct sensor data for touch and sometimes misses subtle errors like half-turned screws. The higher-level language model also slows things down considerably. During trash sorting, the robot stood idle for roughly a third of the total time because it had to wait more than seven seconds on average for the planning model's next computation.
Other labs are also looking for ways to teach robots new tasks with less teleoperation. We covered some of them in our AI Radar #5 on Neolabs.

india-deep-tech-87a5e55c94.fulltext:
Memories.ai is paying people to show robots how to do their jobs. The San Francisco startup supplies first-person video data for robot training, with cameras capturing the hands-on details of preparing food, stocking shelves and repairing equipment.
The company is launching Memories Upload, a global gig-work platform where contributors take paid video-recording tasks to help train robots. Its wearable LUCI Pin camera, developed by Memories.ai, weighs under 45 grams and attaches magnetically to mounts worn on a person’s head, chest or wrist. It captures POV video of the contributors doing various tasks. Two cameras can be paired for stereo capture, providing views that help estimate depth.
Memories.ai says its network recorded more than 1 million hours of first-person video in the platform’s first month in beta and that it aims to collect more than 10 million hours by March 2027. The company was founded by former Meta researchers Shawn Shen and Ben Zhou. The company has raised $16 million in venture capital funding to date, including an $8 million seed round in July 2025 led by Susa Ventures, with investors including Samsung Next, and an $8 million “seed extension” in June this year.
Humanoid robotics startup Figure and Physical Intelligence, a startup that builds AI software “brains” that can control a variety of different types of robots and embodied AI devices, are both exploring how robots can learn from POV video footage. Figure’s Index platform pays people to record everyday tasks for its Helix AI models. Physical Intelligence has tested combining human video with teleoperation data, which is recorded as people control robots remotely, demonstrating how to complete tasks or handle unfamiliar objects and environments. Physical Intelligence co-founder Sergey Levine wrote in a blog post that human video and other supplementary data could provide “a source of knowledge about what can happen in the real world,” complementing data collected by robots themselves.
For a robot learning to make coffee, those recordings could show how someone grips a cup, positions it beneath a grinder and moves it without spilling. Footage from different kitchens, tools and ways of working can expose models to a wider variety of tasks and environments. Developers still work out how to translate those observed movements into actions suited to the robot’s own body.
“Recognizing an activity is different from understanding exactly how a hand grips a tool, moves an object or completes a step, especially when the camera is moving and objects are partly hidden,” Rick Zhuang, director of product and engineering for Cosmos at Nvidia, which works with Memories.ai, told Fortune.
Finding those details in a growing collection of footage is part of the problem Memories.ai is trying to solve. The company uses Nvidia’s Metropolis Video Search and Summarization tools to optimize video streaming and processing. Its video-captioning model is fine-tuned from Cosmos, Nvidia’s family of models for understanding the physical world, and it also uses Cosmos-based models to label actions. The company further trains Cosmos on curated video for customers’ specific tasks, a process known as post-training.
The resulting descriptions are tied to specific moments, letting developers search for an action and retrieve relevant examples without watching hours of recordings. “What stands out is the focus on making everyday human experience searchable and useful for robot learning,” Zhuang said of Memories.ai.
The company says its customers include three of the top five frontier AI labs, alongside robotics developers buying its first-person training data, although the company declined to name these customers citing non-disclosure agreements. Co-founder and CEO Shawn Shen told Fortune that customers increasingly want footage covering a wider range of work environments, tasks and camera angles. Two people making coffee in different kitchens can supply useful variation, he said, even when they are completing the same task. Developers also request wrist-level footage to see interactions that a camera on someone’s head might miss, such as exactly when a hand touches an object.
Adam Scraba, Nvidia’s head of physical AI ecosystem for vision agents, told Fortune that the wide variety of specialized tasks in heavy industry, coupled with the need for highly accurate models, presents one of the field’s hardest challenges.
“The training dataset for Vision AI and video analysis becomes critically important for basically all Physical AI solutions. Developers need to find the right corner-case examples, trust their labels and trace each annotation to the moment it describes,” he said.
Producing labels developers can trust is particularly difficult when hands make subtle movements, objects are partly hidden or the boundary between two actions is unclear, Zhuang said. Those cases make human review and evaluation essential. Human video is most useful alongside robot demonstrations and simulation, he added, helping developers connect observations of human work to actions a robot can perform.
Paying human contractors to provide video in this way can raise privacy concerns. Recordings can potentially capture coworkers, passersby and sensitive information. Memories.ai said camera wearers and coworkers who regularly appear must sign consent forms before recording. Before footage leaves the country where it was captured or reaches customers, the company’s teams use automated tools to obscure other people in the frame and mask identifying details such as badges, screens and license plates. It also manually reviews a sample of frames from each batch to check that these sensitive details have been blurred or obscured.
Update, Nov. 10: This story has been updated to clarify the total amount of money Memories.ai has raised to date and to include information about the company’s June 2026 seed extension round.

climate-energy-78ac6d0e9c.headline: India’s Aditya-L1 unlocks Sun's secrets: How new discovery could help predict solar storms that threaten Earth
climate-energy-78ac6d0e9c.fulltext:
The Sun may be millions of kilometres away, but powerful eruptions on its surface can have consequences for life on Earth. From satellite-based navigation and communication to electricity networks, several technologies people depend on can be affected when these eruptions send enormous amounts of charged particles towards our planet.
India's Aditya-L1 solar mission has helped scientists uncover a previously hidden aspect of how these eruptions behave. The discovery could help researchers better understand how solar storms travel through space and, eventually, improve predictions of when they might reach Earth.
Scientists from the Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA), Bengaluru, found that a solar eruption observed in August 2024 did not expand uniformly like a symmetrical bubble. Instead, it expanded unevenly, developing an asymmetric shape.
The finding, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, challenges a commonly used assumption about how these eruptions expand close to the Sun. Researchers arrived at the conclusion by combining observations from Aditya-L1's Visible Emission Line Coronagraph (VELC), images from 
Nasa
's Solar Dynamics Observatory and three-dimensional modelling.
But why does the shape of an eruption matter? And how could understanding its movement help scientists predict solar storms that can disrupt satellites, navigation systems and power infrastructure?
What are solar eruptions and why do they matter?
The Sun is not a completely stable ball of hot gas. Its magnetic field is constantly changing, creating conditions that can trigger powerful eruptions from its outer atmosphere.
One such phenomenon is a coronal mass ejection (CME). It involves the release of enormous quantities of hot, magnetised plasma from the Sun's outermost atmospheric layer, known as the corona. These eruptions can travel through interplanetary space at high speeds, carrying magnetic fields and charged particles with them.
When a CME is directed towards Earth, it can interact with the planet's magnetic field and trigger a geomagnetic storm. The strength of the disturbance depends on several factors, including the speed and magnetic properties of the incoming eruption.
What are coronal mass ejections?
Such storms are not merely astronomical events. They can affect technologies that modern societies increasingly depend on, particularly those operating in space or relying on satellite-based systems.
Satellites can experience disruptions to their operations and, in severe cases, damage to onboard electronics. Solar activity can also affect radio communications and interfere with the accuracy of satellite-based navigation systems such as GPS. Strong geomagnetic disturbances can induce electrical currents in power transmission networks, potentially putting transformers and other grid equipment under stress.
The effects can extend to aviation, particularly high-frequency radio communications and operations on polar routes, where exposure to space-weather disturbances can be greater.
Chethan Kumar, a space expert and journalist who has extensively covered the extraterrestrial field, said solar storms can affect several systems simultaneously, including electricity supplies, radio signals and satellite-based applications.
“Solar storms are also known to interfere with positioning services, so your GPS can get affected. When GPS gets affected, your air travel becomes less reliable, and it's a cascading effect,” he said.
This makes the ability to monitor and forecast solar activity important for satellite operators, communication networks, aviation authorities and power-grid managers.
However, predicting the behaviour of a CME after it leaves the Sun remains a complex scientific challenge. Scientists need to establish not only where an eruption is heading but also how fast it is moving and how its structure changes as it travels through space.
Why are solar storms difficult to predict?
One of the biggest challenges in studying CMEs is understanding their movement in three dimensions, particularly during the initial stages of an eruption.
Scientists use instruments called coronagraphs to observe CMEs. These instruments block the bright solar disc, allowing researchers to study the much fainter corona and track eruptions as they move away from the Sun.
How Aditya-L1 observed the solar eruption
However, conventional coronagraph images primarily capture movement across the observer's field of view. In other words, they show how an eruption travels across the sky but cannot directly establish how fast the plasma is moving towards or away from the observer.
This missing information is important because a CME is a three-dimensional structure, not a flat object moving across an image.
Two eruptions that appear similar in conventional images could have different three-dimensional shapes and expansion patterns. Their interactions with the surrounding solar wind could therefore differ, potentially affecting how their speeds change during propagation.
Scientists have traditionally relied on observations from multiple spacecraft positioned at different locations to reconstruct the three-dimensional evolution of CMEs. While this provides valuable information, studying eruptions close to the Sun remains particularly challenging because they evolve rapidly during these early stages.
This is where Aditya-L1's VELC instrument offers an additional observational capability.
How Aditya-L1 uncovered the hidden dimension
VELC is one of the primary scientific instruments onboard Aditya-L1. It was developed by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics in Bengaluru, with substantial support from 
Isro
.
Unlike instruments that only capture images, VELC also records spectra, allowing scientists to study changes in the wavelength of light emitted by the solar corona.
The technique is known as Doppler spectroscopy. It is based on the principle that the wavelength of light changes depending on the movement of the source relative to the observer.
For instance, when plasma moves towards an observer, the light it emits shifts towards shorter wavelengths, known as a blue shift. When it moves away, the wavelength shifts towards the longer, red end of the spectrum.
Two observations combined.
This allows scientists to measure movement along the line of sight, the direction between the observed object and the observer, which conventional images cannot directly reveal.
During the CME observed on August 5, 2024, VELC detected an unusual pattern in the spectrum. Researchers observed two distinct branches of emission appearing simultaneously on opposite sides of the regular coronal emission line.
One branch was shifted towards shorter wavelengths, indicating plasma moving towards the observer, while the other shifted towards longer wavelengths, indicating plasma moving away.
The observations suggested that different parts of the expanding CME were moving in opposite directions along the line of sight.
Meanwhile, images captured by Nasa's Solar Dynamics Observatory showed how the eruption was propagating across the sky.
The researchers combined the two sets of observations to understand the eruption's three-dimensional behaviour.
To interpret the unusual spectral pattern, the IIA team developed a three-dimensional geometric and kinematic model of the expanding shell-like CME structure. They varied the model's parameters to determine which configuration could reproduce the observations recorded by VELC.
The results showed that a symmetrical expansion could not adequately explain the observed spectral features. However, when the researchers introduced a tilted structure and asymmetric lateral expansion, the simulated spectra closely matched the actual observations.
The combination of spectroscopic measurements, solar images and three-dimensional modelling provided evidence that the CME had expanded non-uniformly in the low corona, the region of the Sun's outer atmosphere closest to its visible surface.
Why does the shape of a solar eruption matter?
The discovery is important because the shape and expansion of a CME can influence how it travels through the heliosphere, the vast region of space dominated by the Sun's solar wind and magnetic field.
As a CME moves away from the Sun, it interacts with the surrounding solar wind. These interactions can affect its speed, with the solar wind exerting a drag force on the expanding structure.
An eruption's shape and expansion pattern could influence the extent of this interaction. A CME expanding differently in different directions may therefore experience different levels of drag compared with one expanding uniformly.
This can make it more difficult to estimate how its speed will change during its journey towards Earth.
For scientists monitoring space weather, even small differences in the estimated speed and trajectory of a CME can matter when calculating its potential arrival time.
Understanding the eruption's three-dimensional structure close to the Sun could therefore help improve models used to track its subsequent movement through space.
The latest study does not establish that all CMEs expand asymmetrically. It examines one particular eruption observed on August 5, 2024. However, it provides evidence that assuming a symmetrical, bubble-like expansion may not always accurately represent how these structures evolve.
Further observations will be needed to establish how frequently such asymmetric expansion occurs and how significantly it affects CME propagation.
Can satellites protect themselves from solar storms?
Satellite operators make preparations to deal with space-weather events, but these measures have limitations, particularly during very large solar storms.
Kumar said satellites are equipped with thermal protection and operators use space-weather predictions to plan for potential disturbances. When forecasts indicate a threat, operators may attempt to change a satellite's orbit or direction.
“But if there's a massive event, no matter what you do, your planning doesn't work,” he said.
He added that orbit manoeuvres, including moving satellites to a higher orbit or changing their direction, can be expensive and may not always work.
Referring to the impact of solar storms on Starlink satellites, Kumar said there are instances when replacing disrupted satellites can be a more practical option for operators able to launch new ones frequently.
He said the effects of solar storms should not be presented as an inevitable catastrophe for space infrastructure.
Kumar added that solar storms have existed for as long as the Sun and that satellites have been operating for around 70 years. Such events can pose a threat, but that does not mean every satellite will be affected or destroyed when a large CME occurs.
Could Aditya-L1 help improve solar-storm forecasts?
The broader significance of the research lies in its potential contribution to space-weather forecasting.
Scientists need to understand the direction, speed and expansion of a CME to estimate whether it could reach Earth and when it might arrive. Better observations of its early evolution could help refine the models used to make these predictions.
About Aditya-L1
If researchers can reliably reconstruct the three-dimensional geometry of CMEs using VELC's spectroscopic measurements, it could provide an additional way to study eruptions without depending entirely on observations from multiple spacecraft positioned at different vantage points.
This information could eventually be useful for agencies monitoring space weather and organisations responsible for operating satellites, communication networks and power infrastructure.

A Ksheerasagar( with inputs from Deutsche Welle)Published10 Nov 2026, 07:48 PM IST Indian stocks have staged a strong comeback in recent sessions, with benchmark indices witnessing a sustained rally that bulls had been eagerly awaiting since the beginning of the year. While there have been no significant domestic triggers behind the upmove, the rally has largely been driven by the return of foreign investors, who had largely stayed away from Asia's third-largest economy in recent months. Their shift in sentiment comes amid a rotation away from AI-linked stocks, driven by concerns over a slowdown in data center expansion following the Democrats' victories in both houses. A sharp retreat in crude oil prices has also boosted foreign investors' optimism towards Indian equities, prompting FPIs to pour ₹53,739 crore into domestic stocks in November so far, according to NSDL data. The inflows have helped the Nifty 50 extend its winning streak to seven consecutive sessions, enabling the benchmark index to pare its year-to-date losses to 4.15%. The key question now is whether the return of foreign investors signals a durable turnaround or is merely a tactical shift driven by global developments and expectations of tax relief. To understand what is driving the change in FPI sentiment, the possibility of capital gains tax relief, and whether the recent inflows can be sustained, Manoj Purohit, Partner & Leader, Financial Services Tax, Tax & Regulatory Services, BDO India, shared his views. Foreign investors are reassessing their current exposure to India amid ongoing discussions and representations by industry bodies and various associations seeking tax breaks on long-term investments. In addition to expectations of tax relief, the recent US midterm elections could influence the revision and revival of various trade policies. In 2026, to date, FPIs have been constantly exiting the Indian capital market; however, the recent few weeks have witnessed a wait-and-watch approach towards large stake sales in Indian listed companies, as expectations of capital market tax reforms gather momentum. The recent propositions made to the government and positive assurance from the Finance Ministry to express readiness to revisit the taxation framework for long-term investors in the upcoming Budget 2027 have made foreign investors pause and relook at the Indian equity market from a long-term perspective. Investors holding long-term positions with significant unrealised gains are reportedly postponing exits while awaiting clarity on whether the government will rationalise the taxation of equity investments and reduce transaction costs. India is evaluating measures to strengthen its position as a preferred destination for global capital. Discussions among policymakers, regulators, and industry stakeholders have centered on rationalising the Securities Transaction Tax (STT), simplifying capital gains taxation, and providing potential relief under the Long-Term Capital Gains (LTCG) regime for offshore institutional investors. Expectations of a broader overhaul have gathered pace in recent months. Industry expectations are centered around abolishing the current 12.5% LTCG tax on foreign investors' equity investments, resulting in a reduction in tax costs. Industry bodies have echoed similar views and advocated restoring the LTCG exemption on listed securities and enhancing tax certainty, thereby rationalising LTCG, Short-Term Capital Gains (STCG) tax, and STT provisions. Together, these proposals aim to reduce transaction costs, improve market liquidity, deepen capital markets, make it competitive with other jurisdictions that have very minimal or NIL capital gains tax, and attract long-term foreign investment. The discussion on making equity tax reforms lucrative is also relevant given that the revenue authorities had already announced a few favorable tax measures associated with certain debt investments, including specified government securities (G-Secs). With the tax arbitrage between debt and equity tapering, investors are now evaluating asset allocation decisions based on overall post-tax returns rather than considering only the tax outflow. The cautious stance of FPIs also coincides with a more supportive global backdrop. Political developments in the United States have rejuvenated hopes to ease the aggressive trade measures, while expectations of lower global interest rates, strengthening of exchange rates and improved liquidity conditions have strengthened sentiment towards emerging markets, including India. other-interests-79cb5f66bc.headline: Correcting quantum computer errors may be more complicated than expected
other-interests-79cb5f66bc.fulltext:
Quantum computers will not become useful until researchers perfect methods for correcting errors that these devices naturally make. Quantum error-correction (QEC) techniques have advanced rapidly in recent years, but several studies now suggest that the landscape of errors they must tackle is unexpectedly complex, which poses new challenges for making quantum computers practical.
The idea of QEC dates back to the very inception of quantum computing and the first investigations of how quantum computers could be put to work. At that time, no one had built a quantum computer, so researchers relied on mathematical theory to work out how well errors could be corrected, and which computations this error correction would allow the computers to reliably complete. Now, quantum computers do exist and data about their errors is fast accumulating. Increasingly, researchers are finding there are some types of errors that the earlier investigations had overlooked, and they could threaten quantum computers’ progress.
Quantum computers are made from building blocks called qubits, and qubits make errors because they are sensitive to interactions with their environment. One long-standing assumption about these errors – the Markov assumption – has been that they are memoryless: errors that a qubit makes at different points in time are uncorrelated.
Advertisement
Memory effects are detrimental for the useful operation of quantum computers because they mean that making a qubit repeat the same operation at different times may lead to different results based on what its environment “remembers”, says Lorenza Viola at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire. It is as if multiplying a number by 2 gives one value right now and a different value later. The Markov assumption posits that this happens either never or in a small number of cases, which would allow quantum computers to run longer programs. But troublingly, the assumption seems to be incorrect. Memory effects keep appearing in experiments.
Recently, Ioan Pop at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology and Stuttgart University in Germany and his colleagues developed a measurement method that uncovered very long-lived defects – spurious quantum states that arise from material imperfections, stray molecules or several other sources – in a superconducting qubit’s environment, each of which could act as a memory. “We are concretely showing how this long-lived environment can break one of the assumptions of error correction,” he says.
Earlier this year, Rami Barends at Forschungszentrum Jülich GmbH in Germany and his colleagues studied a different type of superconducting qubit and found similar violations of the Markov assumption.
The assumption has been challenged at the level of whole quantum computers, too. In 2025, John Fidel Kam at the Agency for Science, Technology and Research in Singapore, Kavan Modi at the Singapore University of Technology and Design, Muhammad Usman at Monash University in Australia and their colleagues analysed a key error-correction experiment with Google’s Willow quantum computer. They found that some of the errors that were difficult to correct or account for matched a theoretical model in which the Markov assumption didn’t hold. The qubits’ environment was non-Markovian.
In another analysis, Gregory Quiroz at Johns Hopkins University in Maryland and his colleagues discovered that a model including non-Markovian effects represented an IBM quantum computer that they accessed through the cloud seven times better than the noise models commonly used in studies of error-correction. IBM and Google did not respond to New Scientist’s request for comment.
Working with colleagues, Viola has found that the parts of a qubit’s environment that can “remember” can additionally act as quantum systems in their own right and “respond” to a qubit. This introduces a new kind of error – another effect that QEC approaches currently do not account for.
This work is preliminary, but Viola says that as quantum computers are rapidly improving, previously irrelevant effects could become increasingly important. Modi thinks it is too early to sound the alarm, but he says that there are currently no guarantees, experimental or theoretical, that the problem will not worsen as quantum computers grow in qubit number.
“There is a chance that error correction does not work because correlated noise [memory effects] has not been accounted for,” he says. “We don’t fully know where it breaks down, partly because complex noise is hard to describe.”
There are mathematical theorems suggesting that a quantum computer could reach fault-tolerance – a mode of operation where errors do not stymie it – even when there are memory effects and errors are correlated in time or space. But just how strong those correlations can be before they become a problem is another open question, says Viola.
Amit Hagar at Indiana University Bloomington says that the situation isn’t necessarily black and white, and standard error-correction methods could end up working, but only for computations of a certain length or complexity. This would undermine the promise of a quantum computer as a machine that can run arbitrarily long computations. For any firm that is trying to build one, the burden of proof now shifts to their researchers, he says. “They were basing their promise on a theorem, which was conditional, and currently the condition may not work,” says Hagar.
In Usman’s view, the future is rather open because the programs researchers use for quantum error-correction are themselves evolving alongside quantum computing hardware. Until recently, QEC programs that date back to the 1990s were the gold standard, but a whole new class of codes known as QLDPC have now gained traction, and how well they work in the face of correlated errors is not yet clear, he says. “There is a lot more to investigate and study before we make any claim about whether error correction is going to work or not,” he says.
“Error correction codes can adapt to non-Markovian errors. They will have to adapt to that,” says Pop. The measurement technique that he and his colleagues developed recently could play a part here because it may enable other teams to identify memory effects in their devices and devise strategies for avoiding them, says his colleague Nicolas Gosling at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology. Correlated errors could also be mitigated by adjusting conventional computer algorithms that control quantum computers and read their output, says Kam.
So, there are several ways for tackling this neglected class of errors. The researchers who study them say that they haven’t necessarily uncovered an unsolvable problem – as long as it’s taken seriously. “It was not on the radar of many people until now,” says Pop.

Key Points

- In Q3, the Claude developer grew revenue 47 percent to nearly $17 billion and narrowed its net loss, though growth slowed compared to the prior quarter.

Anthropic is hitting the road to pitch investors on its IPO. Despite growing skepticism on Wall Street and massive infrastructure costs, the stock offering could raise up to $90.4 billion.
According to a report from Reuters, AI company Anthropic plans to raise up to $64.4 billion through its public offering. Based on the share count listed in its prospectus, the OpenAI rival is targeting a valuation of up to $1.02 trillion. Details of the plan were briefly sent to investment banks on Monday evening before being pulled back.

deep-tech-b95af7f78b.headline: Google unveils Gemini Robotics 2.5 for factory humanoids
deep-tech-b95af7f78b.fulltext:
Google DeepMind has introduced Gemini Robotics 2.5, its most capable vision-language-action model for robots outside the lab. The company says the release helps machines handle everyday tools and delicate, flexible objects with greater precision in unstructured settings where tasks are less predictable.
Testing centred on dexterity, reliability, and safety across an evaluation set of 200 distinct tasks. The release extends earlier work that brought whole-body intelligence to robots of many types, including humanoids. It also pushes Google deeper into physical AI on the factory floor.
Two models split the work on Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid during a Mercedes-Benz deployment. The embodied reasoning model Gemini Robotics ER tracks the workflow. The Gemini Robotics 2.5 actions model controls the robot’s hands and arms.
At plants in Kecskemét, Hungary, and Sindelfingen, Germany, Apollo 2 performed automotive kitting on active production lines, sorting parts from bulk bins into organised trays in the exact order each vehicle required. This wasn’t a laboratory demo.
Apollo 2 picked and packed automotive parts with a 96 percent success rate during the proof-of-concept. Google DeepMind says robots could take on the monotonous work so technicians can focus on complex build tasks.
Apptronik said in a statement: “This is what we built Apollo for: useful work alongside people in real industrial settings. Pairing Apollo 2 with Gemini Robotics, we saw the models improve dramatically in just a few weeks of post-training and carry over to Mercedes-Benz production with very little drop-off.
“This is the foundation for bringing humanoid robots to industrial and commercial environments at scale.”
Gemini Robotics 2.5 achieves a 30 percent to 100 percent higher success rate than previous baselines, depending on task type, completing the same evaluations 20-30 percent faster. Google reports improved task precision alongside those gains. The company says the model increases both the breadth of skills a robot can learn and the speed at which it acquires them.
The model family also spans hardware beyond humanoids. Apollo 2’s SharpaWave hand offers 22 degrees of freedom; the same software also runs on the Franka Duo platform, which uses parallel grippers. Gemini Robotics 2.5 doesn’t need a humanoid hand, so it isn’t tied to one robot design.
Google credits Gemini 4 Argon with accelerating the underlying research. The system worked as a simulation engine, generating practice runs from camera scenes and building a digital twin of each task so engineers could test why a task failed before applying changes on real robots. That simulation-first method reflects broader enterprise interest in world models.
Inference-time reasoning guidance now steers robots around physical hazards as they move into everyday environments. The new ASIMOV-Jailbreak benchmark measures resistance to disguised unsafe requests across varied scenes.
Argon achieved a 99.5 percent jailbreak resistance rate on the benchmark, a figure Google describes as a substantial improvement over the previous Gemini Robotics ER baseline. It was the strongest resistance result ever recorded.
