deep-tech-dddeeb3826.headline: Google’s Gemini Robotics 2.5 scores 96% in factory trial after tackling 200 tasks
deep-tech-dddeeb3826.fulltext:
Google DeepMind has introduced Gemini Robotics 2.5, a new model designed to help robots learn physical tasks faster, handle delicate objects, and operate more reliably in real-world environments.
The model achieved a 96 percent success rate in a factory proof-of-concept involving Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid robots on Mercedes-Benz production lines. The robots autonomously sorted automotive parts from bulk bins into organized trays, preparing components in the sequence required for vehicle assembly.
The trial took place at production facilities in Kecskemét, Hungary, and Sindelfingen, Germany. Google said the work could help automate repetitive and physically demanding tasks while allowing factory technicians to focus on more complex assembly work.
Gemini Robotics 2.5 is the company’s latest vision-language-action (VLA) model, which translates visual information and instructions into physical robot movements. It is currently rolling out to Google’s robotics partners.
Model tackles 200 tasks
Google evaluated Gemini Robotics 2.5 across more than 200 distinct tasks, including serving food with tongs, tying bows on gift boxes, and transferring liquids with pipettes.
These activities test a range of capabilities, from handling delicate objects to manipulating flexible materials and using everyday tools.
Compared with previous baselines, the model achieved success rates that were 30 percent to 100 percent higher, depending on the task. It also completed activities 20 percent to 30 percent faster, according to Google.

The model works across different robotic platforms, including Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid and the Franka Duo system, which uses two-fingered parallel grippers.
For the Mercedes-Benz demonstration, Google’s embodied reasoning model, Gemini Robotics ER, tracked the workflow, while Gemini Robotics 2.5 controlled the robot’s arms and hands. Apollo 2 picked metal brackets from supply bins and placed them into sequencing containers, adjusting its movements when necessary.
Safety and training advances
Beyond dexterity, Google has improved the model’s ability to navigate physical hazards. Its inference-time reasoning guidance helps robots avoid obstacles and operate around people.
In company evaluations, the capability increased safe task completion by 33 percent around obstacles and 43 percent near people.
Google also introduced ASIMOV-Jailbreak, an open-source benchmark designed to test whether robotic systems can resist disguised unsafe instructions. It contains hundreds of prompts spanning dozens of scenes.
Google reported that Gemini 4 Argon achieved 99.5 percent resistance to these jailbreak attempts, compared with 82 percent for the previous Gemini Robotics ER 2 baseline.
The company also credited Gemini 4 Argon with accelerating the development of its new robotics model. The system can generate thousands of simulated practice runs from real-world camera footage and create digital twins of physical environments.
Researchers can combine these simulations with real training demonstrations to help robots generalize their skills to unfamiliar objects and settings. Argon can also analyze failed attempts and suggest improvements for subsequent training.
The developments mark Google’s latest push to bring more adaptable robots into industrial and everyday environments. However, the 96 percent factory result remains a proof-of-concept, rather than evidence of widespread commercial deployment.

india-a26508bea8.headline: China Is Nibbling at India’s Domination of Bhutan’s Economy - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
india-a26508bea8.source: The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
india-a26508bea8.fulltext:
China and Bhutan have agreed to build on the “positive momentum” in their ongoing efforts to resolve their border dispute. At the 16th Expert Group Meeting (EGM) on the China-Bhutan Boundary Issues held in the Bhutanese capital, Thimphu, on October 13-15, “the two sides reviewed the positive progress made in the China-Bhutan boundary negotiations in recent years.” According to a joint statement issued at the end of the talks, the discussion to “take forward the implementation of the Memorandum of Understanding on the Three-Step Roadmap for Expediting the China-Bhutan Boundary Negotiations” was “friendly, candid and constructive.”
What transpired in the talks has not been made public. Still, the fact that the Sino-Bhutanese talks have made “positive progress” worries India, as some of the territories under Bhutanese control that China is eyeing are of strategic significance to Delhi. How Thimphu and Beijing settle their border dispute, and whether and where Bhutan cedes territory to its giant northern neighbor, will have implications for India’s national security.
Unlike India, which has strong and close relations with Bhutan, China’s ties with Bhutan are weak. The two countries have no official diplomatic relations. They became neighbors only after the PRC annexed Tibet.
However, China’s influence and role in the Himalayan kingdom are growing, which worries India. The territorial dispute between the two countries has cast a long shadow on their relationship.
The Sino-Bhutanese border is around 477 km long. China’s territorial claims have traditionally included 269 sq km in Doklam, Sinchulung, Dramana, and Shakhatoe in western Bhutan; and another 495 sq km in the Jakurlung and Pasamlung Valleys in northern Bhutan. In June 2020, Beijing also claimed the Sakteng Wildlife Sanctuary, an area spanning 650 sq km in the eastern Bhutanese district of Trashigang. Territory in western and eastern Bhutan that China claims holds strategic importance for India, and India is apprehensive that under pressure from China, Bhutan will hand over these territories to Beijing.
The Doklam plateau, for example, oversees the Bhutan-China-India trijunction that is close to India’s Siliguri Corridor, a 24-km-wide corridor wedged between Nepal and Bangladesh, which links the Indian “mainland” to its restive Northeast. Indian military experts say that Doklam in Bhutan’s control gives India a “major terrain advantage” in a military confrontation with China that it would lose should Bhutan cede some territory here to Beijing.
Similarly, the Sakteng sanctuary adjoins West Kameng and Tawang districts in the Indian state of Arunachal Pradesh, where China claims around 90,000 sq km of territory. Control over Tawang — the main bone of contention between India and China in the eastern sector of their disputed border — is critical to India’s defense of not only Arunachal but also the Northeast.
China began articulating its claims over Bhutan is the early 19th century. In 1930, Mao Zedong is said to have named Bhutan, among other countries, as falling within “the correct boundaries of China.”
Following the communist takeover, and especially after the annexation of Tibet, China’s claims over Bhutanese territory grew in stridency. Maps in official publications showed Bhutan as Chinese territory. In 1959, when thousands of Tibetans fled to Bhutan in the wake of China’s crackdown on the Tibetan uprising, the People’s Liberation Army occupied eight Bhutanese enclaves in western Bhutan. That prompted Bhutan to snap ties with China.
China and Bhutan began engaging in talks to settle their border dispute in 1984. The talks made little progress, and it is only in recent years that they seem to have gained pace, especially after October 2021, when the two sides gave the negotiations more structure by agreeing on a three-step roadmap, involving delimitation of the border on maps, joint surveys, and actual demarcation of the border.
Beijing has not relied on talks alone to settle its border dispute with Bhutan. It has been piling up pressure on Bhutan on multiple fronts. It has, for example, been altering the status quo on the ground, despite a 1998 agreement requiring both countries to “refrain from taking any unilateral action to change the status quo of the boundary.”
Beijing has pushed Tibetan grazers and Chinese border patrol teams into Doklam. It has also built roads and other infrastructure inside Bhutan. Satellite images reveal that Beijing has constructed entire villages, roads, hydropower stations, communications facilities, and military and police outposts inside the territory it claims, especially in northern Bhutan.
China is also building economic leverage vis-à-vis Bhutan. A landlocked country, Bhutan is heavily dependent on India for trade, investment, and access to the sea. But China is now nibbling into the Bhutanese economy.
Chinese tourist arrivals, which stood at a meager 1,494 in 2010, rose to 6,167 in 2025. In terms of numbers, the Chinese tourist arrivals are paltry, particularly when compared with other regional tourist destinations. However, it is the rate at which China’s footprint in Bhutan’s economy is growing that should worry Delhi, as it is an important indicator of Beijing’s rising economic leverage in Bhutan.
As for trade, in August 2026, China exported goods worth $14.4 million to Bhutan — a 193 percent increase from August 2025, when trade amounted to $4.93 million. Bhutan’s hunger for Chinese goods is mounting.
China’s role in the Bhutanese economy is all the more significant because these achievements have come without official economic relations between the two countries. As Aditya Gowdara Shivamurthy, an associate fellow in the New Delhi-based Observer Research Foundation, pointed out, the growth in trade has been achieved even though “no infrastructure or mechanism exists for direct trade with China.” Trade is conducted through third countries.
Of course, China’s role in the Bhutanese economy is nowhere near that of India, which is Bhutan’s largest trade partner (India accounts for almost 80 percent of Bhutan’s total trade, and provides a market for 90 percent of its exports) and its biggest source of foreign direct investment. Not only has India built five major hydropower projects in Bhutan, but it is also the largest buyer of Bhutan’s hydropower exports, a major source of revenue for the country. Importantly, geography favors India not China in the Himalayas.
However, India cannot match China’s deep pockets, and it is this advantage that Beijing will lean on as it expands its role, influence, and leverage over Bhutan. As Bhutanese dependence on China grows so will its vulnerability to Chinese pressure on the border issue.
China and Bhutan differ on the sequencing of settling the border dispute and establishing diplomatic relations. Beijing is keen on establishing diplomatic relations first; if not, it would like the two processes to move simultaneously. Thimphu, however, prefers settling the border dispute before it establishes diplomatic ties with China. Perhaps it fears that should diplomatic ties be established first, China’s role and influence in Bhutan will grow at a far faster pace than it is already.
The Bhutanese people, especially those of an older generation, perceive India positively. They are grateful to India for the role it has played in Bhutan’s socio-economic development. However, things are changing in the once-remote Himalayan kingdom. Bhutanese youth are seeing the infrastructure that China has developed in other South Asian countries and also in Tibet. They would like to benefit too from such development.

world-e35600dc82.headline: China Wants India’s Market. Does It Want India’s Industrial Rise?
world-e35600dc82.fulltext:
China’s latest export controls could complicate its economic rapprochement with India. On October 19, Beijing announced export controls on strategic heavy construction and engineering machinery – including tunnel-boring machines and walking excavators – with tougher licensing requirements for destinations involved in disputes with China.
For India, whose metro and high-speed rail projects rely on such machinery, the implications are immediate, including a delay in deliveries for machines manufactured in China by a German company. The new rules, effective November 18, give Beijing another lever over India’s industrial ambitions.
Three days earlier, China proposed adding 40 technologies, including advanced solar manufacturing processes, to its prohibited or restricted export lists. These moves follow years of tightening controls on critical minerals and industrial technology. Several consequential measures, notably the 2025 rare earth restrictions, emerged amid China’s confrontation with the United States.
Yet India has felt their effects acutely. Magnet shortages disrupted Indian automakers, while electronics and clean tech manufacturers struggled to secure equipment and expertise. China’s regulatory arsenal, though developed largely for great power competition, has acquired growing significance for India’s industrial future.
China’s export controls could stymie Indian progress into higher-value manufacturing. India’s production-linked incentives (PLIs) are encouraging investment in batteries, solar energy, and advanced manufacturing. Yet moving into more sophisticated production requires specialized machinery, engineering expertise, and technical know-how, much of which still comes from China. Restrictions on those transfers threaten to slow India’s efforts to develop domestic capabilities.
Chinese strategic commentators have long questioned the wisdom of supplying technology and machinery that could help India emerge as an industrial competitor. Beijing has also challenged Indian subsidies for batteries, EVs, and solar manufacturing at the World Trade Organization. China’s growing list of restrictions on technology exports gives Beijing more ways to act on those longstanding concerns.
Yet restricting India carries a price. India is a major and growing market for Chinese manufacturers, many of which face brutal competition at home and trade barriers in the United States and Europe. Bilateral trade reached a record $155.6 billion in 2025, overwhelmingly in China’s favor: China exported $135.9 billion worth of goods to India. Chinese machinery, components, and expertise are integral to India’s industrial expansion. Therefore, the companies selling them have powerful reasons to keep doing business.
That tension is evident in Chinese-language commentary. Some writers warn that sweeping restrictions would send Indian customers to German, Japanese, or Korean suppliers and accelerate India’s efforts to develop domestic alternatives. Others advocate a more selective approach: continue supplying commercially valuable equipment while guarding the technologies and manufacturing know-how that sustain China’s industrial lead. Yet industrial equipment is a long-term commitment. If Indian buyers cannot count on spare parts, upgrades, and technical support, cheaper Chinese machinery becomes a riskier investment.
The timing is particularly uncomfortable for New Delhi. After years of restrictions on Chinese investment since the Galwan clash in 2020, India eased approval procedures in March for selected manufacturing sectors, including capital goods, electronic components, and solar inputs. Its stated aim was to attract investment, gain access to technology, and connect Indian firms with global supply chains. New Delhi is easing access to Chinese investment just as Beijing tightens controls over technology transfers. Even a Chinese-funded factory approved by India may struggle to obtain the production technology it needs from China.
India may continue expanding its manufacturing base using Chinese equipment. But acquiring the engineering capabilities to produce more sophisticated technologies at home will be increasingly difficult if Beijing restricts access to the expertise it needs.
Beijing, of course, has a calculation of its own. Tighter controls could slow India’s emergence as an industrial competitor while preserving its reliance on Chinese suppliers. Yet excessive restrictions may eventually drive Indian manufacturers toward alternative partners, even at greater cost. Beijing could find that protecting its industrial advantage today comes at the expense of its commercial opportunities in India tomorrow.

Federal Reserve Governor Michelle Bowman said she sees a number of risks to economic activity from financial markets, including a sharp downturn in stock prices if returns on investments in artificial intelligence fall short of expectations.
Speaking in Washington on Tuesday, Bowman flagged the risk of “a large correction in equity valuations” stemming from AI returns, along with “a sharp increase in private longer-term rates.”
Advertisement
“Lower equity prices could undermine the resilience in consumer spending,” she said. “And higher interest rates could further strain interest-rate-sensitive sectors of the economy, like housing and small business investment.”
Bowman also signaled she could support an interest-rate hike at the central bank’s final meeting of the year next month, amid persistently elevated inflation.
“Today I am seeing signs that inflation pressures are persisting, while labor market conditions appear to be firming,” she said. “This indicates that there is still work to do to bring inflation closer to 2%.”
Fed officials left interest rates unchanged at their Oct. 27-28 meeting after raising them by a quarter percentage point in September. That was the first rate hike since 2023 as policymakers seek to cool inflation that has been above their 2% target for more than five years.
Bowman said she backed last month’s decision to hold rates steady in order to give the central bank time to better understand how conditions would evolve and how September’s hike would influence the underlying trends in the economy. But recent inflation data have been hotter than she envisioned, she said in prepared remarks before the Council on Foreign Relations.
“While I continue to expect that several of the factors currently boosting inflation will abate next year, currently inflation has proven to be more persistent than I had anticipated,” she said.
A majority of officials in September signaled at least one more rate increase would be necessary this year, according to their median projection. While several Fed officials have reinforced this view in recent remarks and said hikes can come at a gradual pace, Governor Christopher Waller earlier Tuesday said the Fed should consider raising rates by a larger, half percentage point at its next meeting in December.
Waller’s remarks came just before the Labor Department reported that consumer prices rose by more than expected in October, with core inflation accelerating at a 0.3% pace from a month earlier, meeting the threshold Waller said would fuel the need for a larger sized rate hike.
Separately, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, who also spoke Tuesday, said she still sees the need for at least two quarter-point rate increases. She did not commit to a jumbo-sized hike.
“It remains clear to me, given the current outlook, that the FOMC needs to implement at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases,” Logan said in prepared remarks for a conference in Houston, referring to the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee on which she votes this year.
AI Build-out
In her speech, Bowman also flagged concerns about rapidly rising AI-related debt, with notable gains in corporate bonds, private credit and project finance, on track to exceed $800 billion this year.
“Given their strong credit ratings, hyperscalers and large tech firms have assumed off-balance-sheet liabilities to allow smaller and riskier companies to use them as collateral in asset-based financing for data center construction and the purchase of accelerated computing equipment,” she said. “These connections among AI firms have also been accompanied by hyperscalers and chip designers making equity investments in smaller companies that purchase their products, creating the appearance of circular financing.”

indian-startups-1d149a5f1e.headline: NVIDIA Scandal & AI Selloff In the US: India’s Neocloud Boom Faces Twin Tests
indian-startups-1d149a5f1e.fulltext: The alleged espionage scandal involving NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and the growing scrutiny of the chipmaker’s business dealings with China have added another layer of uncertainty to the global AI infrastructure market already facing questions about its financing model. At the same time, political and regulatory resistance to data centre expansion in the US could slow infrastructure investment, putting pressure on companies that have borrowed heavily to build capacity. While unrelated, these developments present two separate risks to the investment model underpinning the AI infrastructure boom. The first is already visible in the American stock market. Investors have been selling shares of US neocloud companies since September, with CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN witnessing sharp corrections. The selling intensified through October and into November, as concerns mounted over the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending and the debt these companies have taken on. The selloff has only intensified talk of an AI bubble, and neoclouds in India face the risk of getting caught in the middle. Neoclouds – AI infrastructure providers that offer GPU-as-a-service - have emerged as an important part of NVIDIA's AI ecosystem. They provide GPU compute to customers that may not have the scale or resources to build their own infrastructure. Neocloud business models are capital-intensive, with GPU procurement, data centre capacity, and financing arrangements determining how quickly they can scale up. NVIDIA has played a significant role in supporting this ecosystem through strategic investments and financing arrangements, helping expand the market for its chips beyond traditional hyperscalers. India is increasingly becoming part of this infrastructure buildout. That buildout serves two demand pools. One is subsidised compute for domestic startups, researchers and institutions under the IndiaAI Mission, which had onboarded over 45,000 GPUs by June 2026. By August, it had approved 237 projects for subsidised compute, with 93.18 lakh GPU hours sanctioned. The other is commercial workloads from customers willing to pay for guaranteed capacity. The first highlights the scale of the government programme, but sanctioned hours do not necessarily translate into sustained usage. To justify their spending, India’s neoclouds are betting on the second. Among the main Indian players, Yotta plans to spend over $7 Bn on AI infrastructure by the end of FY27 and is targeting a $1.5 Bn IPO, partly to repay debt. ESDS went to the market after the cost of the GPU servers it planned to buy rose from ₹25 Lakh to ₹1.8 Cr. E2E Networks, meanwhile, reported a 411% year-on-year jump in Q2 revenue. Besides these, the likes of NxtGen, NeevCloud and Neysa are also building their neocloud infrastructure in India in anticipation of a big adoption wave. US giant CoreWeave is also entering India as the sole tenant of a planned 240 MW AdaniConneX data centre campus. However, any sustained pressure on its financing or expansion plans could have implications for the project. If concerns in the US around data centre build-up trickle down to India, neoclouds will be one of the first to get hit as a lot of their build-up depends on institutional funding commitment. The question is whether Indian companies will continue to enjoy the financial backing and attract customer commitments to withstand the headwinds if and when they come. No Anchor Customers In India The investment case for US AI infrastructure companies is underpinned by large customers such as Meta and OpenAI, whose scale and long-term compute requirements offer some visibility into future demand. These anchor customers make it easier for infrastructure providers to secure financing and justify large upfront investments. Indian neoclouds, however, do not yet have comparable customer base to underwrite their expansion plans. International customers now account for 75-80% of Yotta’s customer base, partly because they are willing to pay more. Within India, however, the IndiaAI Mission is emerging as an important source of demand, although it utilised less than half its FY26 outlay of ₹10,000 Cr, which has directly impacted hardware procurement and deployment timelines, as Neysa mentioned in one of its blogs. A recent Moneycontrol report highlighted a mismatch in the Indian market: some GPUs are underused, while startups and researchers say fragmented capacity, allocation delays and the type of hardware on offer can make suitable compute difficult to obtain. A headline GPU count may therefore obscure both the quality of available clusters and the path from allocation to actual use. The mismatch makes domestic demand hard to read. The demand exists, but it does not always reach the neoclouds that have built capacity for it. Even well-funded companies are waiting. Juspay, which buys GPUs with its own cash, has been “given commitments that it will take three to six months” to receive them, co-founder and COO Sheetal Lalwani said at a media briefing. When large customers buy and run their own hardware, and smaller ones struggle to find suitable clusters, aggregate capacity figures say little about how much will turn into long-term, paying contracts for neoclouds. Can government-backed compute requirements offer the kind of long-term revenue visibility that hyperscaler contracts provide in the US? Or will Indian neoclouds remain dependent on international customers to sustain utilisation and justify their infrastructure investments? GPU infrastructure requires substantial upfront capital, while the returns depend on sustained utilisation, predictable demand and long-term customer commitments. Notably, government-led regulations as well as citizen pushback could limit data centre build; it even emerged as a major factor for voters in the recent US midterm elections. For Indian neocloud players, which are increasingly catering to foreign and especially US-based clients, could suffer a trickle-down effect. Neocloud stocks, those of Coreweave, Nebius and Iren, among others, battered after the Democratic win in the recent elections. Closer home, ESDS and E2E stocks are already suffering from the second order impact of the sharp selloff in US tech stocks, following the mid-term results. On November 9, ESDS closed at approximately ₹1,147.25, against a September 24 high of ₹1,864.35, while E2E Networks ended at around ₹490.50, significantly lower than its October 14 high of ₹769. The NVIDIA Question NVIDIA’s role in the neocloud ecosystem goes beyond supplying GPUs. Its investments, financing arrangements and partnerships with infrastructure providers have helped bring new compute capacity online. But the relationship varies across Indian companies. NeevCloud said its engagement with NVIDIA covers technical planning, GPU availability and deployment readiness. Procurement, financing and customer contracts are separate arrangements. The company acknowledged the concentration risk of relying on a single technology provider, but said it ties investments to customer commitments and available financing. “The market correction reinforces the need for discipline. We assess each project on its commercial viability and phase investments accordingly,” Narendra Sen, founder of NeevCloud and RackBank Datacenters, told Inc42. ESDS said it has no direct commercial or financing relationship with NVIDIA. The company buys systems from OEMs and system integrators such as Supermicro, Dell, Lenovo and WWT. It has also signed a $1.25 Bn, seven-year agreement with Australia’s Sharon AI. Sharon AI owns and operates an 8,000-GPU cluster, which ESDS uses to serve its domestic and global customers. ESDS plans to explore similar partnerships. “I would separate technology dependence from financial dependence,” said Piyush Somani, founder of ESDS. He pointed out that all of ESDS’s deployed GPU capacity runs on NVIDIA. Financing is a different matter. ESDS commits capex only after a customer has paid at least 35% of the project cost, and only then does it place orders with OEMs or system integrators, Somani said. Both companies say financing for neocloud centres is getting more selective. Lenders and investors now favour projects with confirmed customers, predictable revenues and substantial upfront advances. Sen added that older GPUs could face more pricing pressure as newer generations arrive. This is where the economic model gets complicated. NVIDIA has offered neoclouds worldwide a revenue-sharing and credit-support model in July, but later paused some of the deals, as reported by The Wall Street Journal. Yotta is exploring similar structures where partners fund and own the GPUs, while the company installs and operates them in its data centres and signs customer contracts. Gorilla, the Nasdaq-listed British tech company, is one such partner. In April, the two companies deepened their partnership, adding another $2.8 Bn to an agreement that was initially valued at $500 Mn. Such partnership models depend on GPU rental prices holding up. If compute prices fall or older GPUs lose value faster than expected, who absorbs the loss: the neocloud, the customer or the financing partner? The Jensen Huang Overhang NVIDIA’s chips, software stack and partnerships shape how quickly new compute capacity comes online. That is one of the reasons The Economist has called it the “central bank of AI”. This also highlights growing concerns about the AI ecosystem’s dependence on NVIDIA. On November 8, NVIDIA’s board launched an independent investigation into reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Huang has acknowledged an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be spying for the Chinese government. The NVIDIA board, however, has maintained that it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. Questions about her alleged links to Chinese intelligence, and what they mean for NVIDIA’s China business, remain open. For Indian neoclouds, the direct exposure is less about a change in NVIDIA’s leadership and more about their dependence on globally-sourced GPUs and NVIDIA’s software ecosystem. The Government of India has said its compute ecosystem currently relies on globally-sourced GPUs and any change in chip availability, export controls, pricing or allocation could affect deployment schedules and project economics. There is no evidence yet that the controversy has affected NVIDIA’s relationships with Indian neoclouds. But any fallout for its leadership, China business or financing strategy would hit an ecosystem that leans heavily on NVIDIA’s technology. There are concerns regarding what a potential wider restructuring of NVIDIA might mean for the neocloud business, especially if the build-up of data centres slows down in the US. Incidentally, NVIDIA is set to announce its third quarter earnings on November 17, 2026, and this will reveal much more about the underlying numbers for the data centre business. Will the corporate governance issues have an overhang on the stock till then? In February this year, the fear was that AI would trigger a SaaSpocalypse. Since then, models have advanced and the opportunities have grown bigger, but the concern now is whether the companies building AI infrastructure can carry the debt and capital commitments needed to keep this boom going.

indian-startups-93e3a33f9d.headline: OpenAI acquires Odessia, travel startup created by Sonder founder
indian-startups-93e3a33f9d.fulltext:
OpenAI has acquired an AI travel agent called Odessia, according to Odessia’s founder, Francis Davidson. Davidson says in a post announcing the deal that he’s now working for OpenAI, helping the AI lab with the future of travel.
Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but this looks like an acqui-hire. Davidson’s announcement focused largely on how he built his AI travel agent Odessia by directing teams of AI agents. The year-old Odessia raised a $6 million pre-seed round led by Sequoia and launched its AI travel agent around five months ago. Davidson says that it had helped early adopters plan millions of dollars’ worth of travel, but the tool has already been shut down.
An OpenAI spokesperson confirmed the hire to TechCrunch. “We’re thrilled to welcome Francis to OpenAI. Francis is a proven founder who has built multiple businesses to help people travel, and we’re excited he’s chosen to build with us.”
However the AI lab has not announced new travel-specific products or plans. It does, however, count such companies as Bookings.com, Expedia, and KAYAK as customers or partners. Travel is also one of the main areas that people are using personal AI assistants to help with. And, back in July 2025, when OpenAI launched its ChatGPT agent, it mentioned travel as one of its potential uses.
OpenAI’s spokesperson didn’t have more to share on its plans for travel-related products, except to say that travel is one of the areas that chatbot users frequently ask about. “1.2 billion people turn to ChatGPT each week for help with everyday tasks — from understanding their health, figuring out what to make for dinner, building a budget, and even planning a trip. We see a real opportunity to make these experiences even more useful,” the spokesperson said.
Acquiring Odessia is interesting for another reason. Davidson is well known in the travel industry after he founded a travel startup called Sonder as a college student in 2014. It was sort of like Airbnb, but it focused on short-term leasing of upscale apartments in major cities worldwide. The pandemic badly hurt it, and as it climbed out of that rut, it went public via a SPAC but didn’t raise as much money as it needed, Davidson later said in a post announcing his resignation as CEO in June 2025.
When a key partnership with Marriott fell through, the company went into bankruptcy and wound down. The bankruptcy trustee sold Sonder’s name, trademarks, and website domain in 2026 to TravelAI, and that website operates as a curated guide to the kind of travel rental properties that Sonder was once known for. Prior to its downfall, Davidson had built Sonder into a unicorn with $143 million in revenues. While Sonder was not, ultimately, a success story, Davidson is the kind of battle-scarred founder that Silicon Valley often values.
So we’ll have to wait and see what OpenAI has in store now with travel, now that he’s joined the company.
Note: This story was updated with OpenAI’s comments.

indian-startups-59c12dcc0a.headline: Sarvam appoints former Google Cloud India MD Sashikumar Sreedharan as President and CBO
indian-startups-59c12dcc0a.fulltext:
AI startup Sarvam has appointed former Google Cloud India Managing Director Sashikumar Sreedharan as its President and Chief Business Officer (CBO).
In his new role, Sreedharan will lead the company’s enterprise and government operations and oversee marketing, finance, forward-deployed engineering, service delivery and commercial operations. He will also join Sarvam’s board of directors.
Sreedharan served as Managing Director of Google Cloud India for over a year. His career spans around 35 years, with previous stints at Microsoft India, IBM, Wipro and Happiest Minds Technologies.
Founded in 2023 by Pratyush Kumar and Vivek Raghavan, Sarvam develops foundational AI models, computing infrastructure and enterprise applications.
The startup claims to have more than 100 enterprises and government institutions are building with its full-stack AI offerings.
The appointment comes as Sarvam expands its AI portfolio with products such as Sarvam 105B, Sarvam Vision 2.1, Saaras V4 and Bulbul V4 Flash.
Earlier this year, the company raised $234 million in the first close of its $300 million Series B round at a valuation of $1.5 billion. Its investors include HCLTech, Bessemer Venture Partners, Khosla Ventures and Peak XV Partners.

indian-startups-f6e2533dd3.headline: Google Cloud India MD Shashikumar Sreedharan joins Sarvam as President and CBO
indian-startups-f6e2533dd3.fulltext:
Google Cloud India MD Shashikumar Sreedharan joins Sarvam as President and CBO
Sreedharan will run Sarvam's business across enterprises and government, and widen its work with digital-native companies, developers and partners.
Sarvam, one of the leading artificial intelligence (AI) startups in India, has announced the appointment of Sashikumar Sreedharan as President and Chief Business Officer. Sreeedharan was previously Managing Director - India of Google Cloud.
A blog post by Sarvam said Sreedharan will also be joining as a board member of the company. His responsibilities include leading the business of Sarvam across enterprises and government, and expanding its work with digital native companies, developers and partners. He will also be responsible for marketing, finance, forward deployed engineering, service delivery, and commercial operations.
“India should be a maker of the intelligence the world runs on. For me, joining Sarvam is a commitment to that opportunity. I look forward to working with the team and our customers to build products that become part of how industries and governments operate,” said Sreedharan.
Sreeedharan has more than three decades of experience building and leading technology businesses. Previously, he led Microsoft India’s enterprise business as the managing director for over five years.
Sarvam said the new appointment comes at a time when the startup is growing in scale and scope. It noted that over 100 enterprises and government institutions are building with Sarvam’s full-stack offering.
“The next phase of Sarvam is about advancing our research, developing products loved by people around the world, and building a company that can operate at a much greater scale. Every enterprise should own its AI,” the blog post said.
Sarvam became a unicorn startup after raising $234 million in the first close of its Series B funding round in June 2026. This round valued the company at $1.5 billion and saw participation from investors such as HCLTech, Bessemer Venture Partners, Khosla Ventures and Peak XV Partners.

indian-startups-c9d26eb0c7.headline: AI training startup Mercor valued at $20 billion in latest funding round
indian-startups-c9d26eb0c7.fulltext:
Mercor said on Tuesday it had raised $750 million in a funding round that valued the AI training startup at $20 billion.
The Series D round drew participation from Benchmark, Felicis, Fundomo, Nvidia and funds managed by affiliates of Apollo, among others.
Here are more details:
Investor enthusiasm for AI has fueled a sharp rise in private funding this year, creating a growing group of heavily capitalized startups carrying multibillion-dollar valuations
Mercor, which began as an AI-powered hiring platform, now connects technology companies with subject-matter experts whose knowledge is used to train, test and improve AI models and agents
The San Francisco-based company said it will use the funding to help train and test AI agents on professional tasks
"Every job in the economy will need its own AI agents and every company will need a way to train and evaluate them on its own work," co-CEO Brendan Foody said
According to Crunchbase, AI-driven startups raised $102 billion, or 64% of global venture capital, in the third quarter of 2026
Mercor, which is backed by Jack Dorsey and venture capitalist Peter Thiel, was valued at about $10 billion after raising $350 million in October last year.

ai-fe6d70a180.headline: Oura to acquire AI-native primary care startup Counsel Health for $625M
ai-fe6d70a180.fulltext:
Oura announced on Tuesday that it’s acquiring AI-native primary care company Counsel Health for $625 million. The deal comes a few weeks after Oura postponed its up to $2.2 billion IPO indefinitely, citing “uncertainty in the IPO market.”
Counsel Health is an AI-powered healthcare platform that combines a chat-based medical experience with access to licensed physicians. Its service was integrated into the Oura app in June.
Users can connect with Counsel’s medical AI to get personalized medical advice, and chat with a physician when needed, all within the Oura app. Now, the companies plan to expand on their existing partnership to build across preventative care, acute care, and specialty and chronic care.
While Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, rivals like RingConn and Ultrahuman are emerging to dethrone it, putting pressure on the company to keep innovating. By acquiring Counsel Health, Oura is looking to expand its business and help users access medical care.
“Oura helps members understand their physiology and, with Counsel, they can take action on their health across a range of needs, from quick questions and prescriptions to lab results, chronic care, and referrals,” said Oura CEO Tom Hale in a press release.
Counsel Health raised a $25 million Series A a year ago, led by Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) and GV. PitchBook estimates it had raised a total of $36 million.
Following the acquisition, Oura says Counsel will continue serving existing and new enterprise partners, with the goal of expanding its AI-native care model to more people beyond Oura’s membership.
Counsel CEO Muthu Alagappan will join Oura as chief clinical AI officer, alongside the company’s 70 employees, Bloomberg reports.
“At Counsel, we’ve built medical AI around trust, safety and responsibility, keeping physicians in the loop for clinical decisions,” Alagappan said in the press release. “Oura’s data gives clinicians objective context, trended biometrics, and member engagement to deliver more informed care. From the start, our teams bonded over a joint vision, shared culture, and mission, further solidifying as we negotiated our deal over the past few months.”
The deal is expected to close before the end of 2027.
Oura also announced that its revenue grew 153% year-over-year to $533 million for the quarter ended on September 30. For its fiscal year 2026, Oura generated revenue of approximately $1.75 billion, marking 92% year-over-year growth.
The company reached an $11 billion valuation following a $900 million late-stage funding round in October 2025.

health-tech-778bf4e7de.headline: Oura to acquire AI virtual primary care partner Counsel Health for $625M
health-tech-778bf4e7de.fulltext:
Smart ring maker and health tracking company Oura plans to acquire AI virtual primary care company and business partner Counsel Health for $625 million, the health tech companies announced Tuesday.
The all-cash deal is expected to close before the end of this year, pending customary closing conditions. Bringing Counsel’s platform and capabilities in-house will allow more Oura members to bring their biometric data into a virtual, in-app care encounter, the companies said in their announcement.
“Oura helps members understand their physiology and, with Counsel, they can take action on their health across a range of needs, from quick questions and prescriptions to lab results, chronic care, and referrals,” Tom Hale, CEO of Oura, said. “Together, we can create a new model of care that extends the current healthcare paradigm by delivering an experience that’s more immediate, personalized, and proactive. This is a massive step in our mission to empower people to live healthier, longer, by delivering on the promise of a 24-7 doctor in your pocket.”
Counsel’s model uses text-based, records-informed medical AI encounters to help field and triage users, providing a path to telehealth encounters with the company’s in-house physicians, who are also supported on the backend by a proprietary “Clinician Cockpit” that surfaces relevant clinical data for the encounter. The two-year-old company boasts enterprise partnerships with health plans, provider organizations, employers and other consumer health organizations, for whom it says its approach can reduce costs and improve access to timely care.
Oura is a digital health giant with 5.7 million paid members, whose recently postponed IPO was targeting a $15.6 billion valuation. The company says it is profitable and “growing meaningfully” with 92% year-over-year revenue growth (nearly $1.8 billion) for the fiscal year ended Sept. 30, but ultimately delayed the offering due to “uncertainty” in the market. Its most recent fiscal quarter, ended Sept. 30, included 153% year-over-year revenue growth an adjusted EBITDA of $87 million.
Oura has partnered with Counsel since June, and in September announced a tighter collaboration centered on the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ ACCESS (Advancing Chronic Care with Effective Scalable Solutions) Model, set to begin early next year. The companies have said early data from their partnership show strong care satisfaction among those who saw a physician (4.6 out of 5 average rating), widespread agreement among Counsel members (90%) that use of their Oura data helped improve care, and general Oura member satisfaction (70%) with the onboarding to Counsel’s services.
“At Counsel, we’ve built medical AI around trust, safety and responsibility, keeping physicians in the loop for clinical decisions,” Muthu Alagappan, M.D., founder and CEO of Counsel, said in the announcement. “Oura’s data gives clinicians objective context, trended biometrics, and member engagement to deliver more informed care. From the start, our teams bonded over a joint vision, shared culture, and mission, further solidifying as we negotiated our deal over the past few months.”
Under a new owner, the company will continue to serve its existing enterprise partners while expanding to new customers and broadening its clinical capacity. For the latter, Oura and Counsel said they plan to bolster preventive care via continuous monitoring and proactive guidance; acute care via timely intervention for episodic health issues; and specialty and chronic care management in areas like reproductive health, cardiometabolic health and aging.
“Oura tells members what’s happening in their bodies, and Counsel helps them act on it,” summarized Oura Executive Chairman David Shuman. “This combination expands our addressable market and deepens the value we deliver to every member. This not only increases lifetime value, but Counsel’s enterprise partners also open the door to millions of people beyond our existing member base.”

work-careers-10a57f35b6.headline: H-1B, Green Card update: IBM ends visa sponsorship for most roles in its biggest division; affected worke
work-careers-10a57f35b6.fulltext:
IBM is ending US visa and Green Card sponsorship for most positions in its consulting division, a major development for foreign workers, including Indian professionals, employed by the technology giant.
Bloomberg reported that the decision affects IBM Consulting, the company's largest business division, which employs more than 150,000 people. Workers impacted by the move will have the 
option of continuing their employment with IBM outside the US or leaving the company by the end of the year
. “We have opted to discontinue visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of such roles in IBM Consulting,” an IBM spokesperson said.
The move comes amid the Trump administration's increasing scrutiny of companies hiring foreign workers and its efforts to make the H-1B visa programme more restrictive.
IBM's decision does not amount to a company-wide end to immigration sponsorship. The reported change specifically concerns the majority of roles in its consulting division.
The affected division had previously relied on US high-skilled visa programmes to address skill shortages. 
However, IBM said participation in these programmes had been declining for several years.
An IBM spokesperson said skill availability and client requirements had evolved, prompting the company to reassess its sponsorship policy.
Trump administration's H-1B crackdown
The decision came as President Donald Trump's administration stepped up pressure on technology companies to prioritise American workers and reduce their reliance on foreign labour.
Trump has introduced several measures aimed at making it harder for companies to hire foreign professionals through the H-1B programme. These include a proposed $100,000 fee for certain new H-1B petitions and changes to the annual visa lottery that give greater priority to higher-paid applicants.
Last month, the administration also suspended Microsoft, Adobe and several major outsourcing companies, including Cognizant, Infosys and Tata Consultancy Services, from the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) programme.
PERM is a key step in the employment-based green card process, requiring employers to demonstrate that hiring a foreign worker will not adversely affect US workers' wages and employment opportunities.
The administration accused the companies of abusing the US worker visa system and suspended them indefinitely from participating in the programme.

indian-startups-5c455337f7.headline: Festive boost: D2C startups bag every third funding deal in October
indian-startups-5c455337f7.fulltext:
Indian startup funding witnessed a sharp slowdown in October, but consumer-focused brands showed resilience. D2C startups raised around $200 million during the month, which was nearly 30% of the total $678 million raised by Indian startups.
In terms of deal volume, D2C startups accounted for 36 of the 108 deals recorded in October, which was 33.33% of the total. Their share was higher than the 20.36% recorded in H1 2026, when they secured 125 of the 614 deals, and 21.57% in Q3 2026, with 55 deals out of 255. This points to a growing share of consumer focused brands in India's startup funding activity.

global-economics-22e3ab44e0.headline: Anthropic sets IPO price band at $70-$78, targets valuation of up to $1.4 trillion
global-economics-22e3ab44e0.fulltext:
Written By Rajendra SaxenaPublished10 Nov 2026, 06:08 PM IST
Artificial intelligence (AI) company Anthropic has set a price range of $70 to $78 per share for its proposed initial public offering (IPO), potentially valuing the five-year-old company at up to $1.405 trillion and positioning it for one of the largest stock market debuts.
According to an updated filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Tuesday, Anthropic plans to offer 825 million shares in the IPO. At the upper end of the price band, the company could raise approximately $64.35 billion.
The proposed valuation represents a significant increase from the $965 billion valuation announced by Anthropic during its May funding round. The company is expected to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol 'ANT' later this month.
Despite the scale of the proposed offering, Anthropic faces an uncertain investment environment as it prepares to market its shares to institutional and retail investors.
The latest US midterm election results, which gave Democrats control of Congress, along with the passage of several state-level ballot measures, have raised questions about the future pace of AI infrastructure development.
Concerns are mounting that regulatory and political opposition could slow the expansion of data centres, which require substantial investments in computing infrastructure and electricity.
Investors are also becoming increasingly cautious about AI-related stocks amid concerns that higher interest rates could increase borrowing costs for companies planning large-scale infrastructure investments.
According to earlier reports, some Anthropic investors have become less confident about the company's potential valuation. The AI developer had reportedly considered a $2 trillion valuation, but shareholders recently expressed doubts about achieving even $1.5 trillion, with one investor describing that figure as a 'stretch'.
If completed as scheduled, Anthropic's Nasdaq debut would come approximately five months after SpaceX completed a record-breaking IPO that raised $85.7 billion.
Elon Musk's space exploration and artificial intelligence company currently has a market capitalisation of just under $2 trillion, broadly in line with its valuation at the time of the listing.
Anthropic was founded in 2021 by chief executive Dario Amodei and a group of researchers who left OpenAI. The company has since emerged as one of OpenAI's biggest competitors in the generative AI market.
It is best known for developing the Claude family of AI models and primarily generates revenue by providing AI products and services to businesses.
On Monday, Anthropic unveiled two new AI models, Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2. The launch marked the company's first release of frontier AI models since Amodei called for a slowdown in the pace of AI development in September.
Anthropic said both models underwent extensive safety and alignment testing. The company also developed additional evaluation frameworks and post-launch monitoring tools before making them available.
Anthropic reported revenue of $33.24 billion for the nine months ended September 30, representing an increase of approximately 1,200% from the corresponding period last year.
However, the company also disclosed a net loss of $104 billion during the nine-month period, compared with a loss of $25.1 billion in the same period of 2025.
Anthropic attributed most of the latest reported loss to changes in the fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities.
The company's rapid revenue expansion, financial losses and spending requirements are expected to be key areas of investor scrutiny as it moves towards its highly anticipated public listing.

ReutersUpdated10 Nov 2026, 06:16 PM IST
Anthropic's IPO is set to raise as much as $64.4 billion, a regulatory filing showed on Tuesday, in a landmark test of whether Wall Street's faith in the AI boom outweighs concerns over its risks.
The company is targeting a valuation of up to $1.02 trillion, according to Reuters calculations based on the outstanding shares listed in the filing.
Reuters exclusively reported on Tuesday that Anthropic and some of its investors plan to sell shares in an indicative price band of between $70 and $78 per share.

1

Anthropic’s IPO could raise as much as $64.4 billion, based on the filing cited in the article. The indicative share price range is $70 to $78.
2
What valuation is Anthropic targeting for its IPO?⌵
The main article puts Anthropic’s target valuation at up to $1.02 trillion, based on Reuters’ calculations using the shares listed in the filing.
3
How much could Anthropic raise including its private placement?⌵
Alongside the IPO, Anthropic plans to raise $26 billion through a separate private placement with cornerstone investors. Combined, the IPO and placement could bring in up to $90.4 billion.
4
Why are investors questioning Anthropic’s IPO valuation?⌵
Investors are weighing Anthropic’s rapid growth against concerns about AI investment returns, infrastructure costs, debt and the possibility of regulatory hurdles. Some investors have also viewed higher proposed valuations as difficult to justify.
5
What are the main financial risks Anthropic disclosed ahead of its IPO?⌵
Anthropic’s filing warns that competitors could develop models faster and that AI advances could outpace its safety and security measures. The company also has substantial computing commitments, making its growth dependent on securing significant future capacity.
The company is launching the roadshow for a historic share sale that is expected to set a benchmark for the sector, following years of hype that fueled a massive influx of capital into AI companies.
Anthropic will also raise $26 billion via a separate private placement deal with cornerstone investors including Alphabet's Google, Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, Reuters reported.
Together with investments from cornerstones, which include Broadcom, Micron Technology, Microsoft and TSMC, the Anthropic share offering will raise a total of up to $90.4 billion.
Details of the blockbuster deal were briefly circulated to investment banks before being retracted late on Monday, according to emails seen by Reuters.
The second half of the year has brought a reckoning for the AI boom, as investors question whether returns will justify the massive spending and mounting debt costs in an elevated interest-rate environment.
Concerns are also rising over the sustainability of the investment cycle, with questions around circular financing arrangements, the risk of infrastructure overcapacity and how quickly companies can turn their AI investments into revenue.
The tech-dominated Nasdaq notched its deepest one-day drop in 19 months on Thursday, wiping out trillions in market value on fears of more AI scrutiny, particularly on data center construction, after Democrats' massive gains in the US midterm elections.
Greater oversight and potential regulatory hurdles could complicate the infrastructure buildout underpinning the AI boom.
But Anthropic's growth has so far defied those concerns, propelled by surging demand for its products, particularly its viral Claude models.
Its filing spoke of a vision to "bring forth an age of miracles," even as it warned of existential risks to humanity, laying bare the extraordinary promise and profound uncertainties at the heart of the AI boom.
Potential investors in Anthropic's highly anticipated IPO were pushing for a more attractive valuation to commit to the offering, with some viewing the recently discussed $1.5 trillion valuation as being at the high end of expectations, Reuters has reported.
GROWTH COMES WITH RISKS
Anthropic's net loss narrowed in the third quarter as revenue jumped 47% from a quarter earlier to $16.96 billion, though the pace of growth slowed. It had surged 144% in the prior quarter.
The company attributed the breakneck growth to the rapid adoption of Claude, including specialized products targeting industries such as healthcare, financial services and legal services.
The prospectus outlined a range of risks facing both the company and the technology, warning that competitors could gain an edge by developing models faster and that advances in AI could outpace Anthropic's ability to put adequate safety and security measures in place.
The warnings come amid a growing number of incidents involving "rogue" AI agents that have escaped sandboxed environments and breached private company systems, alongside concerns that increasingly capable AI tools could be used by hackers to penetrate protected networks.
Anthropic's ambitions also come with enormous infrastructure costs. The company has nearly $900 billion in computing commitments with partners including Amazon and Alphabet's Google, highlighting how its rapid growth depends on securing vast amounts of future computing capacity, some of which relies on financing beyond the company's control.
The listing move follows Elon Musk's SpaceX raising $75 billion in the world's largest IPO in June, at a valuation of nearly $1.75 trillion, excluding additional shares purchased by underwriters through the greenshoe option.
Anthropic, locked in a fierce battle for market share with rival OpenAI, was last valued at $965 billion in a private funding round. The company's prominent investors including Altimeter Capital, Dragoneer, Greenoaks and Sequoia Capital.
Anthropic, led by CEO Dario Amodei, was founded in 2021 by a group of researchers who left OpenAI following disagreements over governance and AI safety.
The shares are expected to trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT" after the IPO closes, which would make Anthropic one of the few major companies to go public this fall as higher borrowing costs, geopolitical turmoil and rising bond yields weigh on the IPO market.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading the syndicate of investment banks underwriting the offering.

global-economics-a1514935e7.headline: Anthropic targets valuation of up to $1.4tn in stock market flotation
global-economics-a1514935e7.fulltext:
Anthropic is seeking a valuation of up to $1.4tn (£1.1tn) in its imminent stock market flotation, short of the $2tn that had been expected before investors started to question the durability of the AI boom.
The developer of the Claude chatbot was widely reported to be targeting a $2tn initial public offering on Wall Street but its sights have been set lower, according to a US regulatory filing on Tuesday.
Anthropic is aiming to raise up to $64.4bn by selling 825m shares in the IPO priced up to $78 a share. The California-based company will also raise a further $26bn via a separate private placement deal with cornerstone investors including the Google parent, Alphabet, and the chipmaker Nvidia.
An extra $9.7bn could be raised from a so-called greenshoe offering, which kicks in if investor demand is high and would take the total amount raised by Anthropic to approximately $100bn if the shares sold at the top end of the price range.
At the upper bracket of the $70-$78 per share price range, Anthropic would be worth $1.4tn on a fully diluted basis – which means taking into account all the common shares in the company in existence, including employee stock options.
Trading in Anthropic shares is expected to begin next week.
  
Investor jitters over the AI boom were crystallised last week when the US midterm elections produced victories for datacentre opponents. This has added to already existing concerns, such as how quickly – or if at all – companies can generate a return on their spending on AI infrastructure.
Brian Hopkins, a principal analyst at Forrester Research, said the midterm elections gave investors the chance to correct valuations that they were beginning to have concerns about, because of worries about the financial sustainability of the AI build-out. The election results brought those concerns to a head, Hopkins said.
 
“The market needed an excuse to correct itself a little bit in terms of valuations,” he said. “The US election spook is what has caused it.”
 
As a consequence, Anthropic’s valuation has also been lowered from an anticipated $2tn, he added.
The largest ever stock market listing is Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which joined the US stock market with a valuation of $1.78tn, raising $75bn. The company, whose assets include Musk’s rocket launch business and the X social media platform, is now worth just under $2tn.
However, the $100bn that could be raised in the Anthropic offering will exceed the amount raised by SpaceX.
Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, is selling about $260m worth of shares in the float, as are his six fellow co-founders. At the top of the price range the co-founders’ stakes will be worth more than $18bn each.
A Chinese spying scandal enveloping Nvidia, a cornerstone company for AI investors, also threatens to overshadow the industry but has not affected share prices so far – other than Nvidia’s.
The updated Anthropic filing stated that the company’s annual revenue is now running at $81bn as of 31 October, up $10bn from the previous month.
Anthropic’s main expenditure is on the computing power, from datacentres, that is key to developing and operating its AI systems. According to its prospectus, Anthropic has compute purchase commitments and lease agreements of more than $70bn over the next 12 months and more than $450bn by 2030, with a further $450bn due by 2045.
In a podcast appearance earlier this year, Anthropic’s Amodei explained how compute commitments had to be matched by revenue growth.
“I could buy $1tn of compute that starts at the end of 2027. If my revenue is not $1tn, if it’s even $800bn, there’s no force on Earth, there’s no hedge on Earth, that could stop me from going bankrupt,” he told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel.
On Tuesday the Financial Times reported that the investment bank Goldman Sachs, which is leading the float along with Morgan Stanley, is forecasting Anthropic will generate annual revenues of $600bn by 2030.
